The customer defines value. Our job is to evidence it in their terms.
Causality is easy to claim and hard to support. Say what the data supports.
A value story nobody hears is not value realized.
DiscussionQuestions:
What value story would the customer actually recognize?
Which evidence supports the story, and which part is still only expected?
What next technical action would make the value more real?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical review, business review, or value-realization example and the evidence behind it.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which customer review package would benefit from AI assembly?
What evidence must travel with the value story?
Which next technical action makes the value more credible?

SuggestedTransitions: Move from value language to the evidence package and next technical action.
FallbackGuidance: If evidence sources are unavailable, build the value structure and identify what evidence you would need.
WrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one technical value story and the evidence that will travel with it.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Produce one costed optimization recommendation the customer could act on this quarter.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the recommendation, the cost basis, and the customer response.

SessionIntroduction: This is the session that explains the motion through the CSAM lens: less status assembly, more customer outcome leadership.
KeyTalkingPoints: Huddles are 30 minutes and workflow-led. CSAM work stays human-led: AI helps gather, synthesize, draft and monitor; the CSAM validates context, trust, commitments and customer-facing messages.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted customer success output?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which customer success work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the CSAM judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
ListenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
FallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
ReflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
CommitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am a Customer Success Account Manager at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.

BringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

SessionIntroduction: Success planning is not documentation. It is how the customer and Microsoft agree what progress means.
KeyTalkingPoints: A plan should name outcomes, milestones, owners, risks and review points. AI can draft and inspect the plan, but only the CSAM can validate the customer priority and commitment.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did your success plan last change because the customer's priorities changed?
Which milestone in it would the customer not recognize as theirs?
What is in the plan because it is genuinely the outcome, and what is there because it was easy to measure?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one active customer priority, its current CSP or success-plan notes and the latest review or action list.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which outcome in your plan is stated in the customer's words rather than ours?
Which milestone has drifted without anyone deciding to move it?
What would you remove from the plan today to make it governable?
ListenFor: Listen for plans built around Microsoft milestones rather than customer outcomes, measures chosen because they are available rather than meaningful, owners who have never agreed to their commitment, and plans so long that nobody governs them. Also listen for drift being reported rather than decided.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the plan as it stands to the single outcome you will make observable this week.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the customer, the one outcome you will make observable this week, and what you will remove from the plan to keep it governable.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Make one success plan outcome observable this week, and remove something to keep the plan governable.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the outcome you made measurable and what you removed.

SessionIntroduction: Today is about moving from signal review to intervention. Scores help, but action changes the customer trajectory.
KeyTalkingPoints: Health work spans adoption, usage, support, delivery, sentiment and stakeholder change. The CSAM must separate noise from the risk that matters most right now.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which customer worries you for reasons the health score does not capture?
What did someone say in a recent conversation that has not made it into any system?
Which risk have you been watching rather than acting on, and why?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with visible health, adoption, support or delivery risk and the current owner or open question.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the driver behind the score, not the score itself?
Which signal came from a person rather than a system, and did it survive into the record?
Who owns the intervention, and by when does it have to start to matter?
ListenFor: Listen for health scores treated as the diagnosis rather than the symptom, risks the team has normalized, interventions without owners, and conversation-based signals that never reached the data. Also listen for the customer's own view of their health being absent from the discussion.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the ranked health view to one intervention with an owner, a due date, and an escalation threshold.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the top risk, its actual driver rather than its score, the owner who has agreed to the intervention, and the escalation threshold.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Find the driver behind one health score, then take the intervention to an owner who agrees to it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the driver, the owner, and the escalation threshold you set.

SessionIntroduction: Executive alignment is where customer success becomes visible to the people who can sponsor, unblock or redirect it.
KeyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps should show influence, decision rights, relationship health and the next ask. AI can assemble signals; the CSAM decides the message and timing.
DiscussionQuestions:
Who is the most senior person at this customer you have never spoken to directly?
Which stakeholder could stop this work, and do you know what they care about?
When an executive last engaged, what did they actually want from us?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one upcoming executive or sponsor conversation and the latest stakeholder context.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which stakeholder can stop this, and what do they need to believe?
Where is your coverage a title on a map rather than a relationship?
What would you ask the executive for if you had fifteen minutes tomorrow?
ListenFor: Listen for stakeholder maps built from org charts rather than observed behavior, executive relationships that exist only through an intermediary, engagement plans with no ask, and blockers identified without a plan to reach them. Also listen for assuming a quiet stakeholder is a supportive one.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the stakeholder map to the one relationship you will build this month and the reason they would take the meeting.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the stakeholder you will reach this month, what that person needs to believe, and who can make the introduction.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Reach one stakeholder you have never spoken to directly, and know what they care about before you do.
BringBackEvidence: Bring who you reached, how, and what you learned that you did not expect.

SessionIntroduction: CSAM orchestration is making the customer-success system observable enough to run.
KeyTalkingPoints: Handoffs need an input, owner and date. Escalation is not a failure when it is used to unblock the system and protect customer outcomes.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where does work currently stop between Microsoft, the partner, and the customer?
Who believes they own something that someone else also believes they own?
Which handoff have you personally been compensating for?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one workstream involving Microsoft, customer, partner, support or delivery handoffs.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Where exactly does work stop between the three parties?
Who thinks they own that step, and have you asked them?
What are you personally absorbing because the handoff does not work?
ListenFor: Listen for the CSAM compensating for a broken handoff rather than fixing it, ownership assumed across company boundaries, partner commitments with no date, and coordination meetings that report rather than decide. Also listen for the customer's own team being left out of the orchestration picture.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the coordination map to the one handoff you will make explicit, with both sides named.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the handoff you will make explicit, both parties by name, and the date it will be agreed rather than assumed.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Make one handoff explicit this week by agreeing it with both sides rather than assuming it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the handoff, both owners, and the date it was agreed.

SessionIntroduction: Adoption activity does not automatically become customer value. Today is about proving and accelerating value realization.
KeyTalkingPoints: Adoption plans should link underused features, customer priorities, behavior-change actions, milestones and value evidence. AI can draft the plan and value narrative; the CSAM validates truth and relevance.
DiscussionQuestions:
What value has this customer actually realized that you could prove today?
Where is adoption stalled, and do you know why or are you guessing?
What would the customer say they got, if asked without us in the room?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one workload or solution where adoption progress, friction or value proof needs to be clarified.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What value can you evidence today, and what are you asserting?
Where adoption stalled, do you know the cause or are you inferring it?
Would the customer describe the value the same way you just did?
ListenFor: Listen for value claimed from usage figures alone, adoption barriers guessed rather than investigated, realized value described in Microsoft terms rather than customer outcomes, and proof that would not survive a procurement conversation. Also listen for value stories that have never been said back to the customer.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the value picture to one claim you will evidence, and one adoption barrier you will actually diagnose.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name one value claim you will evidence, one adoption barrier you will diagnose rather than guess at, and how you will say it back to the customer.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Evidence one value claim, and diagnose one adoption barrier instead of guessing at it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the evidenced claim and what you found was actually blocking adoption.

SessionIntroduction: Renewal readiness starts before the renewal motion. Today is about seeing risk and growth conditions early.
KeyTalkingPoints: Consumption, MACC or usage trajectory, adoption gaps, value evidence, support health and stakeholder signals all shape renewal confidence.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which renewal are you least confident about, and what specifically drives that?
What consumption signal would you want to see six months before a renewal conversation?
Where is growth genuinely available versus where are you hoping?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with renewal, consumption, usage or expansion relevance in the near planning horizon.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is your forecast based on, and how far ahead does the signal reach?
Which growth opportunity is supported by consumption evidence?
What would you need to know now to avoid a surprise at renewal?
ListenFor: Listen for forecasts driven by relationship confidence rather than consumption evidence, growth assumed from headroom rather than intent, renewal risk surfacing late because nobody looked early, and commercial ownership blurring between CSAM and CE. Also listen for consumption trends read without seasonality.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the forecast to the one early signal you will start tracking, and who you will align it with.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the renewal you are least confident about, the early signal you will start tracking, and who you will align the forecast with.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Start tracking one early consumption signal and hand it to the account owner.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the signal, why it matters, and who you handed it to.

SessionIntroduction: Escalations test trust. Today is about moving from scattered status to a grounded recovery plan.
KeyTalkingPoints: A useful brief names customer impact, current status, owner, decision needed, next action and update cadence. AI can consolidate threads; the CSAM validates tone, accuracy and accountability.
DiscussionQuestions:
What issue are you currently managing that should probably already be escalated?
What is holding you back: evidence, ownership, or the conversation itself?
When an escalation last worked well, what made it work?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live or recent delivery risk, incident, support issue or overdue commitment.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What threshold would have told you to escalate this a month ago?
What does the recovery plan commit us to, and can we deliver it?
What will you tell the customer, and when?
ListenFor: Listen for escalation delayed to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, recovery plans that promise more than delivery can support, customer communication planned after the internal fix rather than alongside it, and escalations raised without a defined exit. Also listen for the same issue recurring without anyone treating the pattern.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the delivery risk to a recovery plan with an owner, a customer message, and a defined exit condition.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the risk you will escalate or resolve this week, the recovery commitment delivery can actually support, and what the customer will be told.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Take one issue to escalation or resolution this week, with a recovery commitment delivery can actually support.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the issue, the recovery plan, and what the customer was told.

SessionIntroduction: Signals arrive faster than anyone can work them, and the ones you never reach expire without telling you. This session is about being deliberate over which ones you drop.
KeyTalkingPoints: A signal is an unqualified lead until confirmed, not evidence of intent. The windows are real: Contact Me signals carry a 48-hour SLA and preloaded plan priorities a 14-day SLA, with an FY27 target of at least 85 percent of TPP and Sales Accelerator signals actioned. A signal you consciously declined and a signal you never reached look identical in the data and are completely different in practice. Facilitator note: Sales Home is in preview, has only been enabled for individual contributors rather than managers, and its outreach drafting is English only, so some of the room may be working in Sales Accelerator instead.
DiscussionQuestions:
How many signals are sitting in your queue right now that you have not looked at?
When you let a signal go, is that usually a decision or an accident?
What would have to be true for you to confidently ignore a signal?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: open Sales Home or Sales Accelerator and bring your current signal queue, including anything already overdue.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which signal in your queue is closest to expiring and why has it not been touched?
What do you actually know about the account behind it?
Which of your open plan priorities are you never realistically going to work?
ListenFor: Listen for queues sorted by interest rather than by clock, for signals treated as intent rather than as unqualified leads, for outreach planned to contacts who are not in MSX, and for priorities being carried indefinitely because nobody wants to close them.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the triaged queue to the one signal each person will action and the ones they will explicitly close.
FallbackGuidance: If someone's queue is empty or inaccessible, have them work the most recent signal they let expire and reconstruct what they would have needed to act on it in time.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the signal each person will action and at least one they are deliberately closing with a reason recorded.
ReflectPrompt: Which signal did you find you had been avoiding rather than declining?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, action the signal closest to expiry in your queue, and close at least one priority you know you will never work, with the reason written down.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the signal you actioned, what happened, and the reason you recorded on the one you closed.

SessionIntroduction: Handing something to a partner feels like finishing it. The windows say otherwise, and they close whether or not anyone is watching.
KeyTalkingPoints: A referral sent through Accept and Send to Partner creates a lead in Partner Center and notifies both the partner Referrals Admin and the named partner seller. The partner then has 14 days to accept or decline before the lead expires, and 60 days after accepting to qualify, convert to a co-sell opportunity or mark it lost, after which the system marks it lost automatically. Status comes back through the Partner Timeline view on the plan priority. The data-sharing rules are firm: no personally identifiable information without customer consent, no financial or seat-level detail, and no MSX screenshots or exports. After the handoff you remain accountable for account-level orchestration, so a referral that fails is still your account.
DiscussionQuestions:
How many open referrals do you have right now, and when did you last look at them?
What do you actually send a partner when you route something?
When a referral goes quiet, what do you do?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: open the Partner Timeline view on your plan priorities and bring your open referrals with the dates you sent them.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which of the things you are routing would a partner genuinely serve better?
What would the partner need from you that you did not send?
Which of your open referrals is closest to a window closing?
ListenFor: Listen for routing driven by capacity rather than fit, for referral notes too thin for anyone to act on, for internal detail about to cross to a partner, and for referrals nobody has checked since the day they were sent.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the routing decision to the one referral each person will package properly and the one they will chase or close.
FallbackGuidance: If someone has no open referrals, work the last one they sent and reconstruct what the partner would have needed to act on it. The packaging exercise is the transferable part.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the referral each person will send or chase, and anything they are choosing to let expire deliberately rather than by default.
ReflectPrompt: What did you assume the partner already knew that you had never actually told them?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, check every open referral against its window, chase the one closest to closing, and send one new referral with notes a partner could act on without calling you.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the referral you sent, what you included, and what happened to the one you chased.

SessionIntroduction: A territory of roughly fifty accounts cannot be worked account by account, which means most of it is covered by a partner or by nobody. This session is about finding out which.
KeyTalkingPoints: The territory plan is the primary planning construct in this segment, and individual account plans still sit underneath it for Unified and MACC customers. Territory Planning in MSX Plans is shipped and operational, and Partner Center is the partner-facing surface alongside it. Preloaded plan priorities carry a fourteen-day SLA, with an FY27 target of at least eighty-five percent of TPP and Sales Accelerator signals actioned. Facilitator note: coverage model is a property of the account rather than of the seller, so a single territory will usually span Unified, non-Unified and partner-led accounts at the same time.
DiscussionQuestions:
How many accounts are in your territory, and how many did you touch last quarter?
Of the ones you did not touch, how many is a partner genuinely working?
Who would notice if one of your accounts stopped being covered by anyone?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: open your territory in MSX Plans and bring your account list, including the accounts you have not touched this quarter.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which accounts in your territory are you genuinely working, and which are you assuming somebody else has?
What evidence do you have that the partner is actually working the ones you handed over?
Which account would you be most embarrassed to discover nobody has contacted?
ListenFor: Listen for coverage assumed from a referral being sent rather than accepted, for partner coverage claimed without evidence from the Partner Timeline, for territory reads built from memory rather than from the plan, and for the uncovered set being described as small without anyone having counted it.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the coverage read to the specific uncovered accounts, then to what each person will do about one of them.
FallbackGuidance: If someone cannot reach MSX Plans, have them work from their account list and reconstruct the coverage read from what they know, which usually exposes the gap faster anyway.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the number of accounts they believe are covered by nobody, and one they are going to act on.
ReflectPrompt: Which account did you assume was covered until you looked?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, produce a coverage read on your full territory and take one uncovered account either onto your own list or into a partner conversation.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the count of uncovered accounts you found and what you did with one of them.

SessionIntroduction: Eight sessions, each built around one part of the job rather than one tool. This first one is about what is being asked of you and what is not.
KeyTalkingPoints: The motion is about better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake. Every activity names a human checkpoint - the judgment that does not get delegated. The DAE path covers territory, signals, conversations, deals, partner handoff, renewals and portfolio health. Facilitator note: Sales Agent is not available in GCC or DoD environments, and Sales Home is in preview, individual-contributor only and English only, so the room may be working in different surfaces.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where does your week actually go, and how much of it is preparation and triage?
What have you already tried with AI, and what happened?
What would you want back if you got two hours a week?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: no preparation needed. Bring one recent example of something that took longer than it should have.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the part of the job that does not scale to fifty accounts?
Where would you not want AI involved at all?
What would make you distrust an output?
ListenFor: Listen for expectations that the tools will do the judging, for scepticism worth taking seriously rather than arguing with, and for anyone describing a workflow that is already broken without AI.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the general discussion to the one thing each person will try before the next session.
FallbackGuidance: If the group is quiet, ask what they did last week that they would not want to do again.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the account they will run the baseline task against, so it is specific before they leave.
ReflectPrompt: Which part of your week would you most like to stop doing manually?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, open Sales Agent and ask it to summarize one account in your territory that you have not looked at this quarter. Note one thing it told you that you did not know, and one thing it got wrong or could not answer.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the account you tried it on, the thing you did not know, and the thing it got wrong. The failure is the more useful half.

SessionIntroduction: The preparation that makes a customer conversation land is the first thing dropped when the calendar fills. This session is about making it cheap enough to survive.
KeyTalkingPoints: Discovery intent is the same as Enterprise - the Frontier Conversation and BOAT framing still apply - but the time available per account is materially different. Contacts must already exist in MSX before outreach can be drafted against them. Sales Home outreach drafting is English only and in preview. Facilitator note: the execution ask this year includes a large volume of C-suite Frontier conversations, so the pressure is toward more conversations, which makes preparation quality the thing at risk.
DiscussionQuestions:
How long do you actually spend preparing for a customer conversation?
What do you skip when you are short of time?
When did generic preparation last cost you a meeting?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer conversation you have coming up in the next two weeks.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the decision you actually want out of this conversation?
What will they push back on, and do you have an answer?
What are you assuming about who is in the room?
ListenFor: Listen for conversations with no stated outcome, for objections nobody has thought about until now, for stakeholder assumptions drawn from a title rather than a behavior, and for preparation that produces talking points rather than a decision.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the prepared brief to the specific ask each person will make.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has an upcoming conversation, use the last one that did not land and reconstruct what preparation would have changed it.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person state the outcome they want and the fallback ask if they do not get it.
ReflectPrompt: What did you find you were assuming about this customer?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, prepare one customer conversation this way and note whether the objection you anticipated was the one that came up.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you prepared, what actually happened, and where the preparation was wrong.

SessionIntroduction: When a partner is transacting the deal, your view of it is partial by design. This session is about working out what you actually know.
KeyTalkingPoints: Partner-led is structural in this segment rather than optional, and the partner frequently closes. Partner-side activity is not visible in MSX; it returns through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center. A deal progressing well through a partner and a deal that has quietly died look identical from inside our systems. Facilitator note: this is the session where the difference between what the record shows and what is actually happening matters most, and the honest answer is often that nobody has asked the partner recently.
DiscussionQuestions:
How do you currently find out what a partner is doing on a deal?
When did you last discover a deal was dead well after it died?
What do you do differently when the partner is closing?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live deal where a partner is involved in the transaction.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What do you genuinely know about this deal versus what you are inferring from the record?
When did you last speak to the partner about it?
What is the next decision, and who actually makes it?
ListenFor: Listen for partner activity inferred from MSX stage rather than confirmed, for next decisions owned by nobody, for deals described as progressing on the strength of an old conversation, and for reluctance to chase a partner in case it looks like distrust.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the deal read to the one ask each person will take to the partner or the customer.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a partner-involved deal live, use the most recent one that closed and reconstruct where visibility was lost.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the ask each person is making and who they are making it of.
ReflectPrompt: What were you assuming was happening that you have not actually confirmed?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish the real state of one partner-involved deal by asking the partner directly, and record what you learned that the system did not show.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the gap between what MSX said and what the partner said.

SessionIntroduction: Renewals arrive in date order and almost never in risk order. This session is about resorting them.
KeyTalkingPoints: The renewal motion here runs across a book of agreements rather than a single account, on a long workback from the renewal date rather than a conversation in the final quarter. Mid-term expansion is often the more available move: security add-ons, moves from standalone to suite licensing, tier upgrades and Copilot attach. Commercial Executive owns enrollment mechanics, commercial strategy and the renewal structure itself. Facilitator note: at this book size, the renewal that goes wrong is usually one nobody looked at rather than one somebody misjudged.
DiscussionQuestions:
How do you decide which renewal to work first?
How far ahead do you actually start?
Where has an expansion been easier than a new opportunity?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your renewal book with dates, or as much of it as you can see.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which renewal are you working because it is next rather than because it is at risk?
What evidence of delivered value exists for the one closest to its date?
Where is there an expansion sitting inside a renewal you were treating defensively?
ListenFor: Listen for books worked in date order, for value assumed rather than evidenced, for expansion framed as a separate pursuit rather than part of the renewal, and for CE engaged after the structure is already fixed.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the risk-sorted book to the one renewal each person will act on.
FallbackGuidance: If renewal data is not accessible, work from the last renewal that was harder than expected and identify when it first became visible.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the renewal each person is acting on and why it moved up the list.
ReflectPrompt: Which renewal were you going to reach too late?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, sort your renewal book by risk rather than date, act on the highest-risk one, and test one expansion hypothesis inside a renewal you were treating defensively.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the renewal that moved up your list and what you did about it.

SessionIntroduction: You will not notice an account going wrong by looking at it, because you are not looking at most of them. You notice by watching what changed.
KeyTalkingPoints: Portfolio health in this segment is about direction of travel across many accounts rather than deep inspection of a few. Consumption movement of roughly a quarter up or down month on month is the kind of change worth a look. Coverage model is a property of the account rather than of the seller, so one portfolio spans Unified, non-Unified and partner-led accounts with different support behind each. Facilitator note: the technical intervention usually belongs to the D-CSA or a partner, so the DAE judgment here is about noticing and routing rather than fixing.
DiscussionQuestions:
How would you currently find out an account was in trouble?
Which accounts have you not thought about this quarter?
What is the earliest signal you have ever caught?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your account list and any consumption or usage view you have access to.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which accounts changed direction rather than simply being low?
What is the explanation, and is it a real one or a guess?
Which of these is genuinely yours to act on?
ListenFor: Listen for low absolute numbers mistaken for decline, for movement explained by assumption rather than evidence, for accounts being taken on personally that belong with the D-CSA or a partner, and for the uncovered portion going unmentioned.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the movement read to the one account each person acts on and the ones they route.
FallbackGuidance: If consumption data is unavailable, use recorded activity as the movement signal and work from the accounts that have gone quiet.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the account each person is acting on and at least one they are deliberately routing elsewhere.
ReflectPrompt: Which account had changed direction without you noticing?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, identify the accounts in your portfolio that changed direction, act on one, and route one to the D-CSA or a partner with the evidence attached.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the movement you found, what caused it, and what you did.

SessionIntroduction: Eight sessions, each built around one part of the commercial job rather than one tool. This first one is about what is being asked and what is not.
KeyTalkingPoints: The motion is about better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption. Every activity names a human checkpoint - the judgment that is not delegated. In this segment the commercial role covers enrollments, renewals and commercial strategy across a large book, and a substantial share transacts through a partner rather than directly. Facilitator note: Sales Agent is not available in GCC or DoD, and policy and licensing interpretation always routes to the authoritative owner rather than to any agent.
DiscussionQuestions:
How much of your week goes to assembling commercial context rather than deciding anything with it?
How many agreements are you responsible for, and how many did you look at last month?
What have you already tried with AI, and what happened?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: no preparation needed. Bring one piece of commercial work that took longer than it should have.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the commercial work that does not scale to a book this size?
Where would you never want an AI answer?
What would make you distrust an output?
ListenFor: Listen for expectations that an agent will interpret policy, for scepticism worth taking seriously, and for workflows that are already broken without AI.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the discussion to the one thing each person will try before the next session.
FallbackGuidance: If the group is quiet, ask what commercial question they answered most often last month.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the account they will run the baseline task against.
ReflectPrompt: Which part of your commercial week would you most like to stop doing manually?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, open Sales Agent and ask it to summarize the agreement position on one account in your book you have not looked at this quarter. Note one thing you did not know and one thing it got wrong.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the account, the thing you did not know, and the thing it got wrong. The failure is the more useful half.

SessionIntroduction: A renewal you reach in its final quarter is a renewal you can process. A renewal you reach a year out is one you can shape.
KeyTalkingPoints: The renewal motion here is an always-on workback across a book rather than a sequence of individual events, and it starts well over a year ahead of the date. Both EA and CSP agreements are in scope and they behave differently: in CSP the partner holds the transaction and often leads the later stages. Mid-term expansion is frequently the more available move - security add-ons, moves from standalone to suite licensing, tier upgrades and Copilot attach. Facilitator note: the CE owns enrollments, renewals and commercial strategy, and eligibility or pricing interpretation still routes to the authoritative source rather than to an agent.
DiscussionQuestions:
How far ahead do you actually start on a renewal?
Which of your renewals are transacted by a partner rather than by us?
When did a renewal last reach you too late to shape?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your renewal book with dates and agreement types, or as much of it as you can see.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which renewal in your book still has commercial options open, and which has effectively closed?
Where does a partner hold the transaction, and what does that change about your role?
What would you need to know a year out that you currently learn three months out?
ListenFor: Listen for books worked in date order, for CSP renewals treated the same as direct ones, for expansion framed as a separate pursuit, and for the assumption that arriving earlier is not possible.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the sorted book to the one renewal each person will start a workback on.
FallbackGuidance: If renewal data is not accessible, use the last renewal that arrived too late and work out when it first became visible.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the renewal each person is starting a workback on and how far out it is.
ReflectPrompt: Which renewal did you assume you had time on?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, sort your renewal book by where commercial options are still open rather than by date, and start a workback on the earliest one that matters.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the renewal you started on and what you found was already decided.

SessionIntroduction: On a partner-transacted deal you advise on a commercial relationship you do not own. This session is about being precise on which levers are actually yours.
KeyTalkingPoints: A substantial share of commercial motion in this segment runs through CSP, where the partner sells and invoices. That changes the CE role from executing a structure to shaping one somebody else will execute, and the partner frequently leads the later stages. CELA rules govern what can be exchanged with a partner: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: the useful distinction in the room is between advice, enablement and execution - most frustration here comes from trying to execute through someone else.
DiscussionQuestions:
On your last partner-transacted deal, what did you actually control?
Where have you given commercial advice that the partner then did not follow?
What can you not share with a partner, and where does that hurt?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live deal where a partner will transact.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which parts of this structure can you decide, and which can you only recommend?
What would make the partner choose a different structure than the one you would pick?
What does the partner need from you that you have not given them?
ListenFor: Listen for advice framed as instruction, for structures assumed to be adopted because they were recommended, for partner exchange that would breach the data rules, and for frustration that is really about a boundary rather than a partner.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the lever analysis to the one piece of enablement each person will prepare.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live partner-transacted deal, use the most recent one and identify where the structure diverged from the recommendation.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the enablement each person is preparing and who it is for.
ReflectPrompt: Where were you trying to execute through somebody else?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, separate what you control from what you influence on one partner-transacted deal, and give the partner one specific thing that makes the right structure easier for them to sell.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you prepared and whether the partner used it.

SessionIntroduction: Commercial risk in this segment is small, numerous, and usually found at renewal. This session is about finding it earlier.
KeyTalkingPoints: Portfolio-level commercial exposure looks different from the single-deal risk an Enterprise CE inspects: many agreements, each individually modest, where the cost is in the aggregate and in the lateness of discovery. Typical shapes include agreements approaching a date with no engagement, deployed estates that have drifted from what was purchased, and exceptions granted once that have quietly become the expected baseline. Facilitator note: policy and eligibility interpretation always routes to the authoritative owner - the work here is noticing and routing, not ruling.
DiscussionQuestions:
How would you currently find out an agreement was going wrong?
Which of your agreements have you not looked at this quarter?
What commercial problem have you seen repeat across several accounts?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your agreement book and any view you have of what is deployed against it.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Where is the gap between what was bought and what is being used?
Which exception have you granted more than once?
Which of these is genuinely commercial rather than a delivery problem wearing commercial clothes?
ListenFor: Listen for exposure estimated rather than counted, for a repeated exception not recognized as a pattern, for commercial framing applied to delivery problems, and for the largest risks going unmentioned because they are spread thin.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the exposure scan to the one risk each person will act on.
FallbackGuidance: If book-level data is unavailable, work from the last commercial surprise and identify the earliest point it could have been seen.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the risk each person is acting on and what made it the most expensive one.
ReflectPrompt: Which commercial risk had you been treating as somebody else's?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, scan your book for commercial exposure, identify the risk that would cost most if found at renewal, and start one intervention on it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the exposure you found and the intervention you started.

SessionIntroduction: Engagement data tells you someone clicked. This session is about telling the difference between that and someone buying, quickly enough to matter.
KeyTalkingPoints: Highly Engaged and program signals carry a 5-day SLA and are yours to action, while Contact Me signals sit with the account executive. Engagement is a weak proxy for intent: several people engaging is a different thing from one person reading. Declining a signal is a legitimate outcome and is far better than half-working it. Facilitator note: Sales Home is in preview and enabled for individual contributors only, with English-only outreach drafting, so some of the room may be working in Sales Accelerator.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did engagement data last mislead you into pursuing something that was never real?
What does genuine evaluation look like in your solution area, as opposed to interest?
How often do you decline a signal outright, and how does that feel?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one Highly Engaged or program signal in your solution area that you are genuinely unsure about.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What in this engagement pattern would you actually bet on?
Is this one person reading or several people evaluating?
If you route this to a partner, what are you handing them?
ListenFor: Listen for volume of engagement being read as strength of intent, for signals being carried rather than routed or declined, for partner routing decided after the signal has gone cold, and for openings built on how closely the customer has been tracked.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the intent judgment to the routing decision each person will make and record before the window closes.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live signal, use one that was pursued and went nowhere, and work backwards to what in the engagement should have been the warning.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the routing decision each person has taken and the reason, including for anything they are declining.
ReflectPrompt: What did you believe the engagement meant before you looked at it properly?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one engagement signal, decide whether it is real, route or decline it, and record why.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the signal, what you judged, what you decided, and whether the outcome supported your read.

SessionIntroduction: Propensity tells you where your solution area might land. Engagement evidence tells you where something has already started. This session is about not confusing the two.
KeyTalkingPoints: The DSS view runs across solution area rather than across account ownership, so the same territory is being read differently by the DAE and by you. Highly Engaged signals carry a five-day SLA and route to DSS, while Contact Me signals carry forty-eight hours and route to the DAE. Weekly Qualification Progression rotates by solution area and is where this work surfaces. Facilitator note: a propensity score is a model output rather than a customer behavior, and it is worth being explicit about that distinction in the room.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where does your solution area show propensity that you have never acted on?
What is the difference between an account that looks like a fit and one that is showing intent?
How do you currently decide which DAE to spend your time with?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your solution-area view across the territories you support, including propensity indicators and any recent engagement signals.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which of your high-propensity accounts have shown no actual engagement at all?
Where are you spending time because a DAE asked rather than because the evidence supports it?
What would make you drop an account off your solution-area list?
ListenFor: Listen for propensity treated as intent, for effort allocated by relationship rather than evidence, for engagement signals counted without checking whether the contact exists in MSX, and for lists that only ever grow.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the propensity-versus-evidence split to the one account each person takes into qualification progression.
FallbackGuidance: If propensity data is unavailable, have them list the accounts they are actively supporting and work backwards to what evidence justified each one.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the account each person takes forward and one they are removing from their list.
ReflectPrompt: Which account were you working on momentum rather than on evidence?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, separate your solution-area list into propensity-with-evidence and propensity-only, take one of the first into qualification progression, and drop one of the second.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the split you produced, the account you progressed, and the one you dropped.

DiscussionQuestions:
How many territories does your solution area cover?
How do you currently decide which DAE to spend time with?
What have you already tried with AI, and what happened?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: no preparation needed. Bring one example of solution-area work that took longer than it should have.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What part of the specialist job does not scale across this many territories?
Where would you never want an AI answer?
What would make you distrust an output?
ListenFor: Listen for expectations that the tools will do the qualifying, for scepticism worth taking seriously, and for workflows already broken without AI.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the discussion to the one thing each person will try before the next session.
FallbackGuidance: If the group is quiet, ask what question a DAE asked them most often last month.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the account they will run the baseline task against.
ReflectPrompt: Which part of your week would you most like to stop doing manually?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, open Sales Agent and ask it to summarize the solution-area position on one account you support but have not looked at this quarter. Note one thing you did not know and one thing it got wrong.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the account, the thing you did not know, and the thing it got wrong.

SessionIntroduction: You are frequently invited into a conversation you did not scope, for an account you do not own, at short notice. This session is about arriving useful anyway.
KeyTalkingPoints: Discovery intent is the same as Enterprise - Frontier Conversation and BOAT framing still apply - but the specialist usually joins a conversation the DAE arranged and will lead. Contacts must already exist in MSX before outreach can be drafted against them. The boundary matters: the DAE owns the account relationship and the commercial thread, and the DSS is there for solution depth. Facilitator note: the most common failure here is a specialist answering a question the customer did not ask, because they prepared the demo they wanted to give.
DiscussionQuestions:
How much notice do you usually get?
What do you do when you have thirty minutes to prepare?
When did you last talk past what the customer actually wanted?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer conversation you have been asked to join.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the DAE actually trying to achieve in this conversation?
What is the technical objection most likely to come up, and can you answer it?
Where does your contribution end and the DAE's begin?
ListenFor: Listen for preparation aimed at the solution rather than at the customer's decision, for boundaries assumed rather than agreed with the DAE, and for technical answers to commercial questions.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the prepared contribution to the boundary each person will confirm with the DAE.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has an upcoming conversation, use the last one that went sideways and identify what preparation would have changed it.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person state what they will contribute and what they will leave to the DAE.
ReflectPrompt: What were you preparing to say that the customer had not asked about?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, prepare one customer conversation this way and agree the boundary with the DAE beforehand rather than discovering it live.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you prepared, what the customer actually asked, and how close those were.

SessionIntroduction: You do not own the deal. You own one decision inside it. This session is about finding that decision and moving it.
KeyTalkingPoints: The DSS advises rather than owns, so the lever is influence and evidence rather than control. Weekly Qualification Progression rotates by solution area and is where this work surfaces. In this segment a partner is frequently involved in the transaction, which adds a second party whose decisions you also do not control. Facilitator note: the useful frame is that a specialist is accountable for the quality of a decision rather than for the outcome of a deal.
DiscussionQuestions:
On your last stalled opportunity, what was actually blocking it?
Was that blocker yours to move?
What happens when you and the DAE disagree on whether a deal is real?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity in your solution area that is not moving.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the solution decision this deal is waiting on?
What evidence would settle it, and who has to produce that?
What are you doing on this deal that is really the DAE's job?
ListenFor: Listen for specialists carrying account-owner work, for solution decisions that are actually commercial ones, for blockers with no named owner, and for evidence assumed to exist.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the named decision to the one action each person takes inside their own remit.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a stalled opportunity, use the last one that was lost and identify the solution decision that never got made.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the decision each person is moving and the action they are taking.
ReflectPrompt: Where were you doing the account owner's job?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, name the solution decision blocking one opportunity, assemble the evidence it needs, and take one action that sits inside your own remit.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the decision, what you did, and whether it moved.

SessionIntroduction: The fastest way to win the next conversation is to point at a customer like them where it already worked. That evidence has to exist before you need it.
KeyTalkingPoints: A specialist works the same solution area across many accounts, which means proof is reusable in a way it is not for an account owner. In this segment value realization is frequently led by a partner in CSP, so the evidence may sit with them rather than with us. Separate what was deployed from what was used and from what the customer valued - they are three different claims. Facilitator note: anything reused across customers has to be sanitized, and what is unremarkable internally can be sensitive externally.
DiscussionQuestions:
When a customer asks who else has done this, what do you say?
Where is the evidence for your last successful deployment?
What can you not say about one customer to another?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account where your solution area was deployed and you believe it worked.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What can you actually evidence about that deployment, as opposed to believe?
Is the proof yours, the customer's, or the partner's to give?
What would you need to remove before using it with another customer?
ListenFor: Listen for deployment mistaken for value, for proof points that rest on one enthusiastic contact, for partner-held evidence assumed to be available, and for reuse that would breach what can be said about a customer.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the evidence review to the one proof point each person will assemble properly.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a clear success, use one where the outcome was ambiguous and work out what would have made it provable.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the proof point each person is assembling and who has to approve its reuse.
ReflectPrompt: Which success could you not actually evidence?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, assemble one reusable proof point from a deployment in your solution area, sanitized so it can be used with another customer, and confirm who needs to approve that.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the proof point and what you had to remove from it.

SessionIntroduction: Investment should be connected to a real customer barrier, not added as a side process. Today is about the AE’s role in naming the investment hypothesis and routing the next decision.
KeyTalkingPoints: Eligibility, funding, and approval are governed human decisions. AI may help assemble context, status, and evidence, but the AE should not overstate approval or commitment.
DiscussionQuestions: Where could investment remove a barrier? Which part is yours to advance? Who owns the next governed decision?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity or account barrier where investment may be relevant, plus any approved context you can safely use.
FacilitatorQuestions: Where might investment remove a real barrier? What evidence supports that barrier? Who owns eligibility, funding, approval, delivery, or value proof?
ListenFor: Listen for funding implied as approved, hidden open questions, unowned handoffs, and investment ideas not tied to an account priority or decision.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from investment concept to the AE’s next governed action on one live case.
FallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario if live data is not appropriate. Do not infer eligibility, approval, or funding status.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the investment hypothesis, evidence gap, and next governed owner.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Test whether investment could remove one real barrier, then route the next decision without implying approval.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the investment hypothesis, source evidence, open questions, owner, and the next governed action.

SessionIntroduction: AE orchestration works when everyone knows the customer decision, their role, the handoff, and the date. Today is about making that operating model explicit.
KeyTalkingPoints: AEs often lead through influence without direct authority. AI can assemble commitments, role gaps, partner context, and follow-up drafts; the AE decides who to pull in and how to lead the motion.
DiscussionQuestions: Where is the handoff currently vague? Which role or partner is missing? What would reduce follow-up noise this week?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live account or opportunity that depends on multiple Microsoft roles, partners, or delivery handoffs.
FacilitatorQuestions: Which role, partner, or handoff is missing right now? What input does each owner need? What follow-up should be automated or drafted, and what should remain relationship-led?
ListenFor: Listen for responsibility without authority, handoffs assumed rather than confirmed, partner motions added late, and meetings where every role attends but no owner is clear.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from role discussion to an owner/date/input map for one opportunity.
FallbackGuidance: If systems are unavailable, map the handoff chain manually and capture the prompt or workflow to run later.
WrapUpGuidance: Name one handoff, role gap, or partner action you will make explicit this week.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Create or update one account-team operating brief with owners, inputs, dates, and next customer decision.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the role/partner map, handoff list, follow-up message or plan, and what changed after owner validation.

SessionIntroduction: A QBR or executive cadence should not be a status meeting. It should make value, commitments, risks, and strategic asks visible enough for the customer to decide.
KeyTalkingPoints: AI can assemble outcomes, usage signals, open commitments, risks, investments, and expansion plays. The AE validates what the customer would recognize as value and which ask advances the relationship.
DiscussionQuestions: What value has been delivered but not evidenced? Which customer commitment is still open? What strategic ask should the QBR create?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with a QBR, SBR, renewal, or executive follow-up where value evidence matters.
FacilitatorQuestions: What value would the customer recognize? Which outcome is supported by evidence, and which is only expected? What strategic ask should follow from the value story?
ListenFor: Listen for value claims without evidence, QBRs that become status readouts, unsupported causality, missing customer commitments, and expansion asks not tied to outcomes.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from value evidence to the executive brief or QBR ask the AE would actually use.
FallbackGuidance: If evidence sources are unavailable, build the value structure and mark each claim as supported, assumed, or needs review.
WrapUpGuidance: Name one value claim to evidence and one strategic ask to sharpen.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Build one executive value or QBR brief and validate which claims are supported before sharing.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the value/QBR brief, source evidence, unsupported claims removed, strategic asks, and owner for follow-up.

SessionIntroduction: Today is about assess the strategic and technical case for investment without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
KeyTalkingPoints: The goal is A strategic and technical investment assessment with dependencies, readiness, risks, and the next governed decision named. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
DiscussionQuestions:
What technical problem is this investment actually meant to solve?
What would tell you six months from now that it worked?
Which dependency would quietly sink it, and who owns that dependency?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What technical outcome does this investment buy that we could not get otherwise?
What is the observable measure that proves it worked?
Which approval or eligibility question are you assuming rather than confirming?
ListenFor: Listen for the ATS drifting into eligibility, funding, or approval decisions that belong to other owners, success measures that cannot be observed, deployment paths assumed rather than validated, and handoffs to delivery with no re-engagement trigger.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the investment case to the technical evidence it needs and the governed decision that comes next.
FallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the investment, the observable success measure, and the approval question you will route to its correct owner rather than answering themselves.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Test one investment case against its technical dependencies, and route one approval question to its real owner.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the dependency that would sink it and the owner you routed the question to.

SessionIntroduction: Today is about prepare the technical contribution for a customer business review without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
KeyTalkingPoints: The goal is A technical CBR contribution with roadmap points, evidence, risks, decisions, and follow-through. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
DiscussionQuestions:
What technical progress can you evidence, rather than assert?
Where has progress been slower than the customer expected, and how will you say so?
What decision do you want the review to produce?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which technical claim in your contribution can you evidence today?
How will you present the area where progress was slower than promised?
What decision should this review produce, and who makes it?
ListenFor: Listen for progress narrated rather than evidenced, slow areas omitted rather than addressed, roadmap statements that commit the product group, and reviews that end without a decision. Also listen for a technical contribution disconnected from the business outcome the customer cares about.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the technical contribution to the decisions it should trigger, and the evidence each decision requires.
FallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the technical claim you will evidence before the review, and the slow area you will address openly rather than omit.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Evidence one technical claim before your next customer review, and decide how you will address the slowest area.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the evidenced claim and how you handled the area that is behind.

SessionIntroduction: Today is about assess technical health and prioritize risk response without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
KeyTalkingPoints: The goal is A prioritized technical risk response with source signals, owner, intervention, and checkpoint. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which technical risk have you known about for weeks without acting on?
What is stopping you: evidence, ownership, or the conversation itself?
Which risk would the customer say is most urgent, and does it match yours?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which risk is most likely to become an escalation, and what is the earliest signal?
Who owns the intervention, and have they agreed to it?
What would you tell the customer today if you had to raise this now?
ListenFor: Listen for risks ranked by score rather than by consequence, interventions with no named owner, escalation thresholds that were never defined, and risks the team has normalized because they have lived with them. Also listen for signals from conversations that never made it into the system data.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the ranked risk view to one intervention with an owner, a date, and an escalation threshold.
FallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the top technical risk, the intervention, the owner who has agreed to it, and the threshold that would trigger escalation.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Take one technical risk to its owner this week with the intervention and the escalation threshold.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the risk, the owner who accepted it, and the threshold you agreed.

SessionIntroduction: Investment-funded proof work needs scope, success measures, failure-mode awareness, and handoff boundaries before execution begins.
KeyTalkingPoints:
SE owns the technical clarity, not eligibility, policy, commercial, or approval decisions.
Success measures must be observable.
Delivery handoff should state what is decided, what remains open, and when SE must be re-engaged.
DiscussionQuestions:
What technical problem is the investment meant to prove or unblock?
Which success measure is observable enough?
What failure mode would make the investment underdeliver?
PreparationChecklist: Bring a proposed investment-funded proof, workshop, PoC, or scoped engagement and the current technical assumptions.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which technical scope boundary matters most?
Which success measure proves the investment helped?
What failure mode or handoff gap needs to be closed before review?
ListenFor: Listen for eligibility or approval decisions implied by the SE, vague proof measures, hidden open questions, and delivery handoffs without re-engagement triggers.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from investment idea to bounded technical proof package.
FallbackGuidance: If live data is inappropriate, use a sanitized case and do not infer eligibility, funding, policy, or approval status.
WrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one scoped technical proof artifact, success measure, or delivery handoff update.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Define what one investment-funded proof must demonstrate, in measures someone else could verify.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the success measures and the failure mode you named.

SessionIntroduction: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence, and clean handoffs. Today is about the commercial and policy link in that chain.
KeyTalkingPoints: Eligibility, funding, exception, and approval remain human decisions. The CE contribution is to surface commercial and policy dependencies, cite authoritative guidance, and route questions to the right owner.
DiscussionQuestions: Which commercial dependency would slow this investment later? Which decision is genuinely yours? Which question must be routed to an authoritative owner?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one proposed or in-flight investment, customer agreement context, current policy question, and the known owner or approver.
FacilitatorQuestions: Which activity helps clarify the commercial or policy dependency? What would make the output safe to use? Where must a human owner decide?
ListenFor: Listen for: eligibility, funding, or approval implied rather than decided; exception ownership unclear; handoffs without named owners; and questions that need authoritative guidance.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the investment lifecycle to the CE-owned dependency and the next governed action.
FallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario. Do not use live customer data or infer eligibility, approval, exception, or funding status.
WrapUpGuidance: Map one investment dependency to the authoritative question, owner, and next human decision.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Map the approval dependencies for one investment and find where it is actually waiting.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the dependency map and the blocker you identified.

SessionIntroduction: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Today is about your part of that chain.
KeyTalkingPoints:
Every role owns one link. The chain breaks at the handoff.
Eligibility, funding and approval are human decisions. AI assembles the evidence.
An investment request without named open questions hides them rather than resolving them.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where could investment-funded scope become undeliverable?
Which prerequisite, dependency, or owner must be confirmed before delivery starts?
What technical outcome evidence will be needed later?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one proposed or approved investment-funded scope, known technical dependencies, and the delivery checkpoints you would want confirmed.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which investment activity is closest to your real delivery responsibility?
What status or milestone data must be verified before acting?
Where could handoff, prerequisite, or ownership failure become customer-visible?
ListenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: funding or approval inferred from summaries; delivery status not checked against the authoritative record; unowned prerequisites; and technical outcomes that cannot be measured later.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the investment lifecycle to the CSA's delivery-readiness or outcome-evidence action on a live or sanitized case.
FallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario. Do not use live customer data or infer eligibility, approval or funding status.
WrapUpGuidance: Name one investment delivery-readiness check or outcome-evidence action and its owner.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Validate delivery readiness for one investment and name the dependency most likely to slip.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the readiness assessment and the dependency you flagged.

SessionIntroduction: Customer investment should be governed through the success plan, not treated as a separate administrative process.
KeyTalkingPoints: Investment execution needs owners, milestones, handoffs, risk tracking and value evidence. The CSAM governs the operating rhythm and realization story.
DiscussionQuestions:
Is the investment on this account connected to the success plan, or running beside it?
Who owns delivery, and when did you last confirm status with them rather than assume it?
What evidence would the realization review need that you do not have yet?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one active or proposed customer investment, scope, milestone list or execution question.
FacilitatorQuestions:
How does this investment show up in the success plan?
Which delivery status did you confirm rather than assume?
What evidence will the realization review need, and who is producing it?
ListenFor: Listen for investment running as a parallel process rather than part of the success plan, delivery status inferred from silence, realization evidence identified only when the review is booked, and the CSAM answering eligibility or approval questions that belong elsewhere.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the investment rhythm to the one checkpoint you will run this month and the evidence it produces.
FallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the investment checkpoint you will run, the delivery status you will confirm rather than assume, and the realization evidence you will start collecting.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Run one investment checkpoint and confirm a delivery status rather than assuming it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the status you confirmed and how it differed from what you assumed.

SessionIntroduction: Today is about align partner and specialist support to technical priorities without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
KeyTalkingPoints: The goal is A partner and specialist alignment plan with feature gaps, owners, timing, and next decision. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where is technical feature the constraint, rather than time or priority?
When you last brought in a specialist, did it change the outcome?
What would a partner need from you to arrive useful rather than catching up?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Is the gap feature, capacity, or clarity? They need different answers.
What exactly would you ask this partner or specialist to do?
What will you send them so they arrive useful rather than catching up?
