ListenFor: Listen for support requested by habit rather than by need, asks vague enough that anyone could decline them politely, briefings promised verbally and never sent, and customer-sensitive detail heading to an external partner without a classification step.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the feature gap to one specific, dated ask with the briefing that makes it answerable.
FallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the feature gap, the specific ask you will send, who receives it, and whether that recipient is internal or external.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Write one specific partner or specialist ask and send the briefing that makes it answerable.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the ask, the briefing, and whether the recipient was internal or external.

SessionIntroduction: Investment requests slow down when inputs, owners, or open questions are hidden. Today is about readiness.
KeyTalkingPoints: Separate facts from assumptions. Name confirmed inputs, gaps, contributors, policy/process questions, and next governed action.
DiscussionQuestions: Which request input is missing? Who owns it? What should not be represented as approved?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
FacilitatorQuestions: What request input is missing? Who owns it? What decision must remain human?
ListenFor: Listen for eligibility or funding implied rather than confirmed, hidden open questions, and contributor inputs without owners.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from request readiness to next governed action.
FallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario if live investment data should not be used.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the next governed investment action, owner, and evidence needed.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Check one investment request against what a complete submission needs before you submit it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what was missing and where the request sits now.

SessionIntroduction: This huddle has no pre-written workflow. The team chooses one, which means the value depends entirely on picking a workflow people actually run. Anchor the session in real work and trusted context before anyone opens a tool.
KeyTalkingPoints:
The workflow must be recurring, not a one-off.
Someone in the room must actually own it.
A specific recent example beats a general description.
If the team cannot name a real example, the workflow is too abstract to work on.
DiscussionQuestions:
What workflow are we improving today?
What triggers it, and how often does it run?
What inputs, constraints, and approvals shape it?
Whose work is it, and who else depends on the output?
PreparationChecklist: Bring one recurring workflow you personally run and one recent example of it, including what made that run harder than it needed to be.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Where in this workflow is effort or quality lost today?
What is the smallest step AI could assist, rather than the whole workflow?
What must a person verify before the output is used?
What would a one-week version of this experiment look like?
ListenFor: Listen for scope that is too broad to test in a week, inputs the person cannot actually access, an output nobody would notice if it were wrong, and enthusiasm for a tool without a workflow behind it. Also listen for the opposite problem: a step so small that automating it changes nothing.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the friction people named to one specific assistable step, then from that step to a single bounded experiment with an owner.
FallbackGuidance: If a tool or data source is unavailable, map the workflow on paper and design the experiment for later execution. Use a hypothetical process shape if needed, but do not invent business facts, customer detail, or system behavior.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the workflow you chose, the one step you will test, the human checkpoint you will keep, and the evidence you will bring back. If you cannot name an owner or a date, the experiment is not real yet; shrink it until it is.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: What will you test this week? State the input, the action, the output, who reviews it, and what would tell you to stop.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the actual output from your experiment, whether it worked or not. A failed experiment with evidence is more useful to the group than a success without it.

SessionIntroduction: Deal making features live inside Sales Agent. There is no separate agent to select: when you ask Sales a deal-related question, those features answer. This session is not about learning to run deals. It is about being able to find deal facts for your own accounts, whatever your role, instead of waiting for someone to send them to you.
KeyTalkingPoints:
Deal Agent is a skill inside Sales Chat, reached by picking the Sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot. There is nothing separate to install or select.
Its primary motion is renewals, specifically EA and MCA-E. That is where it is strongest.
The trigger is specificity. A TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number returns real data; a vague account reference returns a generic answer.
Keep one chat thread per deal. Mixing several deals into one thread confuses the context and makes the history hard to audit.
Looking up deal facts is open to every role. Commercial decisions, approvals, and material amendments are not.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did you last need agreement, licensing, or renewal information and have to ask someone for it?
How long did that take, and what did you do while waiting?
What have you assumed about a customer's entitlements that you have never actually verified?
PreparationChecklist: Bring one real account you work on, and if you have it, an agreement number, enrollment number, or TPID. If you do not have an identifier, bring the account name and we will find one in the session.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What did the lookup return that you did not already know?
What did you previously assume about this customer's estate that turned out to be wrong or unverified?
Where does this stop being your call and become the deal owner's?
ListenFor: Listen for vague prompts producing vague answers, which is the most common reason people conclude deal making does not work. Listen for a first response being treated as final on a complex deal, when the guidance is to re-run and verify against current data. Listen for several unrelated deals being worked in one chat thread. Listen for someone treating a retrieved figure as approved pricing or a commitment, or stepping past retrieval into structuring a deal that belongs to the AE or Commercial Executive. Also listen for the opposite: someone escalating a question they could now answer themselves.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the lookup you ran to the single fact that changes how you would open your next conversation with that customer.
FallbackGuidance: If Sales Agent access is unavailable or a lookup returns nothing, work from an account you know and list what you would need to verify before the next customer conversation, then name who currently holds each answer. Do not guess at entitlements, pricing, or discount levels.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the account you looked up, the one fact that surprised you, and one question you previously would have escalated but can now answer yourself. If nothing was new, pick a less familiar account before the next session.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: What will you do this week? Look up one account before a real customer conversation and use one retrieved fact in that conversation.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the prompt you used, what came back, and whether it changed how the conversation went. If the lookup returned nothing useful, bring the prompt so the group can sharpen it.

SessionIntroduction: Most accounts already carry a satisfaction signal the seller has never looked at. This session is about reading it, deciding whether it matches the relationship you think you have, and acting while the conversation is still yours to lead.
KeyTalkingPoints: CX Vitals sits inside Sales Agent with no setup and covers accounts mapped to a TPID. It is read-only and Microsoft internal, so it informs your judgment and never reaches the customer. The score shows the symptom; the account team knows the cause.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which account are you most confident about, and when did you last check that confidence against data?
Where would a satisfaction score and your own read of the relationship disagree?
Who tells you first today when a customer becomes unhappy?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account you own with its TPID, confirm Sales Agent access, and write down how you would rate that customer's satisfaction before you look at any data.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Where did the data disagree with your own read, and which one do you trust?
Which of the causes you found do you actually own, and which belong to support or delivery?
What would have to get worse before you escalate this?
ListenFor: Listen for sellers treating a score as a diagnosis rather than a symptom, for accounts written off as fine without evidence, for surprise at what verbatims say, and for anyone about to take an internal metric into a customer conversation.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the account picture to the single account each person will act on this week.
FallbackGuidance: If an account is not TPID-mapped there will be no CX data. Use that as the discussion: how would you assess satisfaction without it, and what would you rely on instead.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the account each person will act on and the specific intervention, not a general intention to watch it.
ReflectPrompt: What did the data tell you about a customer that you did not already know, and what will you do differently because of it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, run a CX health summary on the account you are least certain about, and take one action on what you find.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the account, what the data showed versus what you expected, the action you took, and whether the cause turned out to be what the data suggested.

SessionIntroduction: Every seller in this room has inherited an account with nothing useful written down, and every seller has handed one over. This session is about the transition you are in the middle of right now, on either side of it.
KeyTalkingPoints: Enterprise transitions are expected to complete within 30 days of the record being created, and 60 days for SME&C, CASA and Elevate. The transition record is closed only after the customer meeting has happened, not when the fields are populated. There is no mandatory transition document; the requirement is current contacts, a current plan, and a documented customer conversation.
DiscussionQuestions:
What is the worst account you have ever inherited, and what specifically was missing?
What do you know about your accounts that exists nowhere in MSX?
When a customer is handed a new seller, what does it actually cost them?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account you are currently inheriting or handing over. If you have neither, bring the account you would find hardest to hand to someone else.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What did the record fail to tell you that you needed?
What do you know that would be lost if you handed this account over tomorrow?
What would this customer say if you asked them how the last transition went?
ListenFor: Listen for transitions treated as administration rather than as a customer experience, for records closed before the customer meeting happened, for verbal commitments nobody has captured, and for sellers assuming an empty risk field means there is no risk.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from what the record is missing to the one conversation each person needs to have this week, internal or customer-facing.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live transition, run it on the account each person would find hardest to hand over. The exercise of naming what is unwritten works either way.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the account and the specific next conversation, internal or customer. A transition moves when someone talks, not when a field is updated.
ReflectPrompt: What did you find missing from an account record that you assumed would be there, and what will you write down differently because of it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, record one thing about an account you own that currently exists only in your own head.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the account, what you found missing, the conversation you had, and what you recorded so the next person does not have to ask.

SessionIntroduction: Work rarely stalls inside a role. It stalls in the gap between two, where the sending role believes it is done and the receiving role cannot act. This session is about closing that gap on one live handoff.
KeyTalkingPoints: Ownership transfers between the account, specialist and customer success teams are expected to complete within seven business days. A handoff is not complete when ownership changes; it is complete when the receiving role can act. The record is what the next person works from, not the conversation.
DiscussionQuestions:
What is the least useful handoff you have ever received, and what was missing?
When you hand something over, what do you assume the other person already knows?
How would you know today if a handoff you sent had gone nowhere?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity or milestone you are currently handing over or have recently received. If you have neither, bring the one that went worst.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Could the receiving role act on what you sent, without asking you anything?
Where in your own list has a transfer stalled with nobody owning it?
What do you know about this opportunity that is written nowhere?
ListenFor: Listen for handoffs described as notifications, for ownership that changed without anyone accepting it, for milestones carrying placeholder values or dates, and for sellers rebuilding a thin handoff silently rather than sending it back.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the gap analysis to the one handoff each person will prepare, repair or chase this week.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live handoff, use one that has already completed and ask whether the receiving role could have acted on it. The gaps are just as visible in hindsight.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the handoff each person will complete or repair, and who they need to speak to.
ReflectPrompt: What did you assume the receiving role already knew, and what will you write down next time instead of assuming?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one handoff you have sent or received and make it complete enough that the other role could act without contacting you.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the handoff, what was missing, what you added, and whether the receiving role could then act.

SessionIntroduction: A customer commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. This session is about the plan that converts one into the other, and about being honest where that plan has stopped being real.
KeyTalkingPoints: The ATS owns the technical plan behind the consumption number. Milestones without a named owner and a dependency-aware date are forecasts, not plans. Deployment and usage are different measures, and only one of them renews.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your accounts has committed spend that is not converting, and do you know technically why?
Which milestone dates in your current plan would you personally bet on?
Where has something been deployed that nobody is actually using?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with a consumption commitment, the current plan if one exists, and the most recent consumption data you can reach.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Is your baseline a number the account team would agree with?
Which milestone carries most of the gap, and who actually owns it?
Where has deployment completed without usage following?
ListenFor: Listen for baselines nobody has agreed, dates set without checking the dependency beneath them, teams named as owners instead of people, and deployment milestones being treated as evidence of adoption.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the baseline to the single milestone each ATS will resequence or re-own this week.
FallbackGuidance: If consumption data is not reachable for an account, build the milestone sequence from the commitment and the known dependencies, and note the data gap as the first thing to close.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the milestone each person will re-own or resequence, and the dependency they need to confirm.
ReflectPrompt: Which date in your plan turned out to rest on an unconfirmed dependency, and what did you do about it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, confirm one milestone date with the person who owns the dependency behind it, and change the date if they cannot commit.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, the dependency, what the owner said, and whether the date survived the conversation.

SessionIntroduction: Every account plan claims executive sponsorship. Far fewer accounts have someone senior who would actually spend their own credibility to unblock something. This session is about finding out which kind you have.
KeyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps age quietly; the person you are counting on may have changed role or priority. Sponsorship is built over quarters and cannot be assembled in the week you need it. An executive relationship you only use when you need something is not sponsorship.
DiscussionQuestions:
Who on your biggest account would take your call today, and when did you last test that?
Which senior relationship are you assuming is stronger than it is?
When did a sponsor last change without you noticing?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account you feel confident about, and its current stakeholder map. Confidence is what makes this exercise useful.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which recorded sponsor has not actually engaged recently?
Which relationship would hold under pressure, and what is your evidence?
What could you offer that this executive cannot easily get elsewhere?
ListenFor: Listen for sponsorship asserted without evidence, for relationships described by meeting frequency rather than by what the person has done, for engagement plans that would suit any executive at any company, and for sellers softening a weak relationship rather than naming it.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the tested map to the one relationship each person will act on, and what they will offer.
FallbackGuidance: If engagement data is unavailable, run it from memory: name each senior stakeholder and what they have actually done for the account. The honesty of the input matters more than the data source.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the executive each person will engage and what they will offer, not what they will ask for.
ReflectPrompt: Which relationship turned out to be thinner than you assumed, and what will you do about it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one assumed executive relationship by offering something useful and seeing what comes back.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the relationship, what you offered, what the response told you, and whether the sponsorship is real.

SessionIntroduction: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. This session tests that claim against arithmetic, while there is still time to do something about the answer.
KeyTalkingPoints: Fiscal year planning, quota acknowledgment and territory review are annual obligations, and territory reviews recur later in the year. The plan is what you will be held to, so it is worth being the person who finds its weakest assumption first.
DiscussionQuestions:
Do you know, arithmetically, whether your pipeline covers your number?
What single deal or renewal is your year most dependent on?
What support would actually change your position, and have you asked for it specifically?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your quota, your current pipeline by stage, and your renewal base. Bring real numbers; the exercise does not work on estimates.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is your uncovered gap, and by when would new pipeline have to exist to close it?
Where is the growth evidence strongest, and does it match where you spend your time?
What is the one assumption your plan cannot survive without?
ListenFor: Listen for optimistic conversion rates used to make a plan look covered, for growth ranked by familiarity rather than evidence, for concentration risk nobody has named, and for support asks phrased as a general complaint about difficulty.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the coverage gap to the specific, evidenced support request each person will make.
FallbackGuidance: If pipeline data is incomplete, run the arithmetic on what is known and treat the missing part as the first finding. An incomplete pipeline view is itself a planning problem.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the coverage gap and the specific support ask each person will make, to a named person, by a date.
ReflectPrompt: What did the arithmetic tell you that your instinct had not, and what changes because of it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take your coverage gap to your manager or territory review with a specific evidenced ask rather than a general concern.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the gap, the ask you made, who you made it to, and what came back.

SessionIntroduction: Everyone in this room has rebuilt something a colleague had already solved, and everyone has had their own work rebuilt by someone else. This session is about breaking that cycle with one thing you have already made.
KeyTalkingPoints: The best reuse candidate is the thing you keep sending to people, not the thing you are proudest of. An asset without prerequisites and limitations will be used once and abandoned. An asset nobody owns is one nobody trusts.
DiscussionQuestions:
What have you sent to more than one colleague in the last month?
What have you rebuilt that you suspect someone else had already done?
What would you need to see before you trusted a colleague's asset enough to use it with a customer?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one thing you have built that worked, ideally something you have already shared with at least one person.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What in your asset only makes sense because of what you already know?
What would you have to tell someone before they could safely use it?
What does it genuinely not do?
ListenFor: Listen for assets chosen because the author is proud of them rather than because they are repeatedly needed, for customer detail nobody has noticed, for limitations left unstated, and for material about to be stored where only its author would look.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the chosen asset to what each person must write down before anyone else could use it.
FallbackGuidance: If someone has nothing built, have them take a prompt they run repeatedly. The packaging exercise is identical and the reuse value is often higher.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the asset each person will publish and where they will put it. An asset that stays in a personal folder has not been captured.
ReflectPrompt: What did you have to explain about your own work that you had never noticed you were assuming?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, publish one asset with its purpose, prerequisites, limitations and your name on it, somewhere a colleague would look.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the asset, where you put it, what you had to strip out, and whether anyone has used it.

SessionIntroduction: You inherit milestones the customer has committed to, and you are measured on whether they complete. This session is about finding the ones that are quietly not going to land, while there is still time.
KeyTalkingPoints: A milestone status is a claim, not evidence. Committed milestones transfer to customer success to be driven to completion, which means to real usage rather than to a completion flag. Most stalls sit on the customer side, and those conversations go badly when they sound like Microsoft chasing its own number.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your committed milestones would you actually bet on landing?
When a milestone stalls, how long does it usually take you to find out?
Which completed milestone do you suspect nobody is using?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with committed milestones you own, their current dates, and whatever delivery or consumption data you can reach.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which milestone has a status but no evidence behind it?
What is actually blocking the one that stopped, and who owns that?
Where has something completed without anyone using it?
ListenFor: Listen for status fields treated as evidence, for causes guessed at rather than confirmed, for milestones escalated to the wrong owner, and for phased rollouts being mistaken for failed adoption.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the milestone review to the single stalled milestone each person will diagnose and route this week.
FallbackGuidance: If delivery data is not reachable, work from the milestone dates and recent customer engagement alone, and treat the missing data as the first thing to fix.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the stalled milestone each person will diagnose and the owner they will route it to with evidence attached.
ReflectPrompt: Which milestone turned out to be stalled for a different reason than you assumed, and what did that change?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one committed milestone with no supporting evidence and find out what is actually happening with it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, what you assumed was blocking it, what was actually blocking it, and who you routed it to.

SessionIntroduction: Committing a milestone is a one-way door. Everything after it is measured against the date and the value you put on it. This session is about the moment before that door closes.
KeyTalkingPoints: A milestone is ready to commit when there is a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, an agreed value and date, confirmed feasibility, available customer and delivery resources, an available budget and a chosen delivery model. A populated field is not evidence. Once the milestone is committed it transfers to customer success to be driven to completion, so what you commit becomes someone else's number to defend.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your uncommitted milestones would you personally defend the date on?
When a milestone gets committed early, what usually forces it?
Which committed milestone in your patch was committed before it was ready, and what did that cost?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with uncommitted milestones you own, and for one of them the sponsor, the value, the date and how you arrived at each.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which commitment criteria are populated on your milestone but not actually evidenced?
Would your sponsor defend this date to their own leadership?
Which single assumption is carrying most of your value?
ListenFor: Listen for a named contact being treated as an agreed sponsor, for values built from scope assumptions nobody has tested, for dates set from when the number is needed rather than when the work can be done, and for milestones being carried rather than closed.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the readiness read to the single milestone each person will either take to a sponsor or deliberately hold.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has an uncommitted milestone in front of them, use one that was committed and missed, and run the same criteria backwards to find which one failed.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the milestone each person will take forward and the criterion they still have to close, or the milestone they are choosing to hold and why.
ReflectPrompt: Which commitment criterion did you find you had been treating as met without evidence?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one uncommitted milestone and either close the weakest criterion or make the case for holding it, and write the reason into the record either way.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, the criterion that was weakest, what you did about it, and whether it moved.

SessionIntroduction: You are usually the person in the room who knows whether the date is achievable. This session is about the window where saying so still changes the outcome rather than explaining the miss.
KeyTalkingPoints: Feasibility, resources and the delivery model are part of what makes a milestone committable, and they are the part most often assumed. A pattern that worked at another customer is a hypothesis here, not a proven fact. A proof of concept proves what it tested and nothing else, and it gets retold as broader than it was.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which milestone in your patch has a date nobody has worked backwards from?
What is the last thing you assumed the customer would provide and they did not?
Where has a pilot result been repeated back to you as more than it actually showed?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one uncommitted milestone with a technical dependency you are not certain about, along with whatever has been proven so far and what has not.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which part of your technical basis is confirmed here, as opposed to confirmed somewhere else?
What does the customer have to provide, and has anyone actually asked them?
What did your proof deliberately not test?
ListenFor: Listen for patterns from other customers being treated as confirmed, for customer-side resource being assumed rather than secured, for proof results described more broadly than their scope, and for durations being guessed rather than supplied.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the confirmed-versus-assumed split to the one dependency each person will secure or escalate before the date is committed.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has an uncommitted milestone, take a committed one whose date is at risk and run the same split. The output is the same and the urgency is higher.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the assumption or dependency each person will settle, and the position they will give the account team in the meantime.
ReflectPrompt: Which assumption were you carrying as a fact until you had to write it down?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take the assumption carrying most of a milestone date and either settle it or tell the account team plainly that it is open.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the assumption, what you did to settle it, what you found, and how the account team reacted to being told it was open.

SessionIntroduction: Year end generates a lot of urgency and only some of it is real. This session separates the part that is genuinely fixed by the calendar from the part that only feels that way, and acts on the first while there is still room.
KeyTalkingPoints: There is no single worldwide month-by-month year-end calendar for Enterprise sellers, and looking for one is why people end up inventing deadlines. What is genuinely fixed is the systems close: for the FY26 close, licensing and agreement detail had to be submitted by 26 June, all revenue had to reach MS Sales by close of business on 30 June, and the close publish landed on 2 July, after which only limited fields remain editable. Confirm this year's exact dates locally, because they shift by a few days. For a deal to book in a period it must be fully approved, final and fully executed before the end of the last day of that period, and it needs processing runway on top of that. Renewals expiring on the final day of a period are treated differently by the booking and billing calendars and need deliberate handling. Facilitator note: ECIF publishes its own detailed year-end milestone calendar, but the milestone quarter-end validation warning is documented for the Americas only, so do not present it as a worldwide rule.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of the things you are rushing right now would still be urgent if it were March?
What did you find out too late at the last year end?
Which deal did you pull forward last year, and what did it cost to do it?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your own patch or one account, the deals and renewals you expect to land in this period, and a written list of everything you are currently treating as year-end urgent.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which of your in-period deals is waiting on Microsoft, and which is waiting on the customer?
What could you correct today that stops being correctable after close?
Which of your urgent items has a deadline you could actually point to?
ListenFor: Listen for signature dates being treated as booking dates with no processing runway, for renewals at the period boundary assumed to be fine, for corrections being deferred to the week when every queue is longest, and for deadlines whose only source is that it is June.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the closeable list to the single record each person will correct and the single deal each person will deliberately release into the new year.
FallbackGuidance: If someone carries no quota and no renewals, run the third practice only. The record-correction window applies to anyone who owns milestones or agreement detail, and it is the part most often left to somebody else.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming, for each person, one record they will correct before cutoff and one thing they are deliberately not forcing into this period.
ReflectPrompt: Which of your year-end deadlines turned out to have no source other than the month it is?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, correct one record that stops being correctable at close, and tell one customer or one internal owner that a deal you had been pushing is landing in the new year instead.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the record you corrected, the deal you released, and what happened when you said so.

SessionIntroduction: Partner deals rarely fail loudly. They sit at a respectable stage while nothing underneath them moves, and nobody asks because the number does not look wrong.
KeyTalkingPoints: The co-sell stages run Created and Accepted at 10 percent, Qualified at 20, Developed at 40, Proposed at 60, Negotiated at 80 and Won at 100. Partners set their own stages and have every reason to be optimistic, so a stage is a claim rather than evidence. Your accountability is visibility and Stage 2 to 3 acceleration rather than execution ownership; the partner owns delivery in the later stages and partner performance issues belong with the partner development manager. Facilitator note: Partner Center is a separate system from MSX, so the agent cannot read it - sellers must bring their own stage data into the session.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your partner deals would you actually bet on at the stage it claims?
Where do your deals most often stop moving?
When did you last ask a partner for a specific commitment rather than an update?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: pull the current co-sell stage of your pinned-partner deals from Partner Center, with when each last moved.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which stage is ahead of what the partner has actually described?
What is genuinely blocking the one that stopped?
What is the single thing you would ask this partner to commit to?
ListenFor: Listen for recorded stages treated as evidence, for causes assumed rather than confirmed, for partner performance problems being worked one deal at a time instead of raised with the PDM, and for conversations planned with several asks and therefore no ask.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the stage review to the one stalled deal each person will take into their next partner conversation with a specific ask.
FallbackGuidance: If Partner Center data is not to hand, work from what each partner last told you and treat the missing data as the first thing to fix.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the deal each person will raise, the single ask they will make, and what they are offering in return.
ReflectPrompt: Which deal turned out to be stalled for a different reason than the one you had been assuming?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one stalled partner deal into a partner conversation with a single specific ask and something offered in return.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the deal, the ask you made, what the partner committed to, and whether the stage moved.

SessionIntroduction: You cover more accounts than you can work. This session is about making that a set of decisions rather than something that happens to you.
KeyTalkingPoints: Coverage in this role runs at roughly one architect to fifty pinned accounts, which means most accounts will not receive individual attention in any given month and some will receive none at all. Naming those deliberately is the job. A consumption movement is a shape, not a cause: a decline during a planned migration and a decline from a failed deployment look the same in the data, and a rise can be a workload running hotter than the customer intended. Deployed is not used, and the milestone that completed and then flatlined is the one discussed at renewal. Facilitator note: Unified accounts are covered by customer success and cloud solution architects; this role covers the non-Unified pinned base alongside partners, so routing to a partner is a normal outcome rather than an escalation.
DiscussionQuestions:
How many of your accounts did you personally touch last month, out of how many?
When consumption drops on an account, how do you currently decide whether to look?
Which accounts are you quietly hoping nobody asks you about?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your portfolio's recent consumption movement, and an honest number for how many accounts you can realistically work yourself this month.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which of these movements can you already explain, and which genuinely need you?
Which accounts are you routing to a partner, and does that partner actually cover the workload?
Which accounts is nobody working?
ListenFor: Listen for sharp movements being treated as automatically bad, for rises assumed to be good news, for splits that quietly assume more capacity than the person just said they had, for partner routing without checking partner capability, and for reluctance to name the accounts nobody is covering.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the triaged portfolio to the single milestone each person will drive from deployed to actually used.
FallbackGuidance: If consumption data is not to hand, work from the accounts each person already suspects are drifting. The triage judgment is the transferable part and the missing data becomes the first thing to fix.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the accounts each person is personally working this month, the ones going to a partner, and the ones nobody is covering.
ReflectPrompt: Which account did you find you had been assuming someone else was covering?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one committed milestone that completed without producing usage and find out why, then start the intervention.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, what you thought was blocking it, what actually was, and what you did about it.

SessionIntroduction: Someone who was not in any of your discovery conversations is going to build what you designed. This session is about finding out whether they can, while there is still time to change it.
KeyTalkingPoints: Technical design in this segment is largely the same job as anywhere else, with one difference that changes everything downstream: partner delivery capacity is engaged earlier, and the partner owns delivery in the later stages. That means a design is not finished when it is technically sound, it is finished when someone else can build it from what is written. The design in your head is always more complete than the one on the page, and the gap between them is invisible to the person who wrote it. At territory volume, the proofs you decline and the designs you make reusable are what create room for the work that matters.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did a partner last build something differently from what you intended, and where did the misunderstanding start?
What do you know about your current design that is not written down anywhere?
When did you last agree to a proof of concept that did not change anyone's mind?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one design a partner will deliver, and whatever you know about that partner's capability and delivery history.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What would a competent engineer guess wrong about, reading only what you wrote?
Do you actually have evidence this partner can build this, or a certification that suggests it?
What single uncertainty would that proof resolve?
ListenFor: Listen for verbal customer constraints that never reached the document, for partner capability inferred from certification rather than from delivery history, for proofs agreed to because they were asked for rather than because they would settle something, and for designs described as reusable that hide a decision behind every section.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the design gaps to the one thing each person will write down or ask the partner before delivery starts.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live design, use one a partner has already built and work backwards to where the misunderstanding started. The gap-finding exercise is the transferable part and hindsight makes it sharper.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the gap each person will close and whether they are changing the design, changing the partner, or asking a question before delivery starts.
ReflectPrompt: What did you have to explain about your own design that you had not realized you were assuming?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one design a partner will deliver and either write down the context they are missing or ask them the question that would change it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the design, the gap you found, what you did about it, and what the partner said when you raised it.

SessionIntroduction: Partners agree to joint plans in the meeting and then work the deals that pay them. This session is about building a plan that survives that.
KeyTalkingPoints: Formal joint planning is structurally required in this segment rather than being optional assistance. Partner Center is the partner-facing surface and sits outside what our agents can reach, so partner-side status has to be read there directly or through the Partner Timeline view on the plan priority. CELA rules govern the exchange: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits, and signals shared with partners are unqualified leads until confirmed. Facilitator note: the fourteen-day accept window and the sixty-day convert window are system-enforced, so a plan that assumes a slower partner rhythm will lose leads automatically.
DiscussionQuestions:
When a joint plan fails, is it usually capacity, incentive or attention?
What do you actually know about what else your partner is carrying?
What can you not share with a partner, and where does that boundary get uncomfortable?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one current joint plan and, if you have it, a read on what that partner has accepted and converted recently.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What in this plan depends on partner capacity you have never confirmed?
Where does the plan pay the partner less than the alternative work they could be doing?
What would tell you early that the partner has quietly deprioritized this?
ListenFor: Listen for capacity inferred from enthusiasm, for plans that assume a partner rhythm faster than the fourteen and sixty day windows allow, for data being prepared for partner exchange that CELA rules exclude, and for the absence of any trigger that would reveal drift.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the capacity and incentive test to the specific trigger each person will set.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live joint plan, use the most recent partner engagement that underdelivered and reconstruct which of capacity, incentive or attention actually caused it.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the assumption each person is going to confirm with their partner and the trigger they are setting.
ReflectPrompt: What did you assume about your partner's capacity that you have never actually asked?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one joint plan assumption directly with the partner and set a named trigger that would tell you the plan has stopped being true.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what the partner said about capacity and the trigger you set.

SessionIntroduction: This is the first of eight huddles, and the one with no AI activity in it. Today is about what the motion is and what it asks of you. Frontier Accelerator exists because we are asking customers to reshape how they work around AI, and that argument is stronger when we have done it ourselves first. That is what Customer Zero means here: we apply these tools to our own real work, and we are straight about where they help and where they do not.
KeyTalkingPoints:
Weekly and short, led by the manager with a facilitator. The cadence carries the motion, so if the slot has to move, move it rather than drop it.
Four principles hold every week: keep the weekly rhythm, learn from what colleagues have actually tried, ground every session in real work rather than hypothetical scenarios, and try something between huddles so there is an experience to bring back.
Every huddle from next week runs to the same shape, and the agenda and timings are set out on the huddle page: a short framing of why the topic matters, then sharing what you tried since last time, then hands-on work on a real scenario, then a close where you pick the one thing you will carry into the week.
Five roles make the motion work. The Leader connects it to strategy and clears barriers. The Manager owns the huddle and opens with the why. The Facilitator runs it and draws every voice in. The Team Member experiments in their own workflow and brings back wins and friction. The Coach reviews patterns across huddles and feeds insight back.
The journey ahead: this week you get grounded, weeks two to eight you build the habit on real work, week nine the team decides which habits stick and what comes next, and from week ten you choose your own topics.
You are here as a peer, not an expert. You do not need prior AI experience, and “I do not know” is a good answer.
Two things on feedback. The facilitator posts one question in the chat each week, asking how useful the huddle was on a scale of one to ten. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes to improve the sessions, so keep confidential detail out of the room, whether that is customer, partner, enrollment or commercial, and put product problems into the tool's own feedback control rather than here.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you deliberately avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted output in front of a customer?
What would make thirty minutes a week worth protecting for this?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: complete the baseline survey if it has been sent to you, confirm the huddle series is on your calendar, confirm you can open at least one of the tools named for your path, since the commitment at the end of this session runs in one of them, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. If your access is blocked, come anyway and say so, because that is a different problem from not being interested. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which work do you repeat every week without ever thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where does your judgment have to stay human no matter how good the output gets?
What would have to happen in these thirty minutes for you to want the next one?
ListenFor: Listen for unvoiced skepticism, for access blockers stated as disinterest, and for the assumption that this is a tool rollout. Listen for people describing only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat, because the recurring and unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping. Listen for anyone who thinks they need to be an AI expert to take part, and correct that in the room.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
FallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the conversation and record access blockers separately from interest, since they need different fixes. The discovery prompt runs in whichever tool the person already has. If the room stays quiet, start with your own example of work you repeat every week.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the discovery prompt below. Week one is for finding the recurring work worth handing to AI. Post the usefulness question in the chat before people leave.
ReflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
CommitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

“I am a [your role] at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with.”
BringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

SessionIntroduction: Somebody has usually asked this customer most of your questions already. This session is about finding out what they said before you ask again.
KeyTalkingPoints: In this segment a partner is frequently engaged before the engineer is, and may have run discovery of their own. The DAE owns the account relationship and the DSS covers the solution area, so three people may hold pieces of the same picture. Partner-side conversations are not in MSX and return through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center. Facilitator note: the failure mode here is not missing information, it is asking for information somebody already has, which reads to the customer as a team that does not talk to itself.
DiscussionQuestions:
How do you currently find out what has already been asked?
When did you last repeat a question the customer had already answered?
What do you need to establish yourself, whatever anyone else has done?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer where you are about to start technical discovery.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What does the record already tell you about this customer's estate?
Who else has spoken to them, and what would they know that is not written down?
What must you see for yourself rather than take on trust?
ListenFor: Listen for discovery restarted from scratch out of habit, for partner-held knowledge assumed to be unavailable rather than asked for, for the record treated as complete, and for engineers accepting a second-hand answer on something they will be accountable for.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from what is already known to the short list only this person can establish.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has upcoming discovery, use the last engagement where something important surfaced late and work out who already knew it.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one thing each person will ask a colleague or partner rather than the customer.
ReflectPrompt: What were you about to ask a customer that somebody on your own side already knew?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish what is already known about one customer's estate from the record and from whoever else is engaged, and take only your genuinely unanswered questions to the customer.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you learned without asking the customer, and what you still had to ask.

SessionIntroduction: Building a bespoke proof for every customer does not survive contact with this many customers. This session is about proving the point with less.
KeyTalkingPoints: Enterprise engineers can afford a tailored proof per pursuit; at this customer count that arithmetic does not work, so reuse is the constraint rather than a nice-to-have. A partner may be able to run the proof instead, which is covered separately in the design session. What matters here is deciding the smallest thing that would actually settle the customer's doubt. Facilitator note: the most common failure is building a technically impressive proof of something the customer was never doubting.
DiscussionQuestions:
How long does a proof take you, and how many can you run at once?
When did you last build something that already existed?
What was the customer actually unsure about?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer asking for a demo, pilot or proof.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What decision is this proof supposed to settle?
Does something already exist that would settle it?
What is the smallest version that would still be convincing?
ListenFor: Listen for proofs scoped to what is interesting to build rather than to what is in doubt, for reuse dismissed without looking, for success criteria that were never agreed with the customer, and for effort that exceeds the value of the deal.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the decision in doubt to what each person will reuse or scope.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live request, use the last proof that was built and work out what the smallest sufficient version would have been.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is reusing rather than building.
ReflectPrompt: What did you build that you could have borrowed?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, name the decision one customer's proof must settle, look for something that already exists before building anything, and scope the smallest sufficient version.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you found already existing, and what you still had to build.

SessionIntroduction: Most technical questions reach you second-hand, and your answer goes back the same way. This session is about writing for the relay.
KeyTalkingPoints: At this scale the engineer is frequently not in the room. A partner or a seller carries the question in and the answer back, which means the question has already been through one translation before you see it and the answer goes through another on the way out. CELA rules govern what may be exchanged with a partner: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: an answer that requires your presence to make sense is not finished, because you will not be there.
DiscussionQuestions:
How often are you answering a question the customer asked somebody else?
When has an answer of yours arrived at a customer distorted?
What do you put in writing differently when a partner will forward it?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical question that reached you through somebody else.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What do you think the customer actually asked, as opposed to what reached you?
Which part of your answer would you least like to see paraphrased?
What would this look like if the person relaying it did not understand it?
ListenFor: Listen for the relayed question taken at face value, for answers written for a technical peer rather than for the relayer, for caveats that will not survive being summarized, and for detail that CELA rules exclude from partner exchange.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the reconstructed question to the answer each person will write for relay.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live question, use one that came back a second time and work out what was lost in the first answer.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the part of each answer that must not be paraphrased.
ReflectPrompt: Which of your answers has been repeated to a customer in a form you would not recognize?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, answer one relayed technical question in a form that survives being forwarded, and mark explicitly what must be passed on word for word.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the answer you wrote and what came back.

SessionIntroduction: You will not notice a customer's technical problem by looking at them, because you are not looking at most of them and you do not operate any of it. You notice by recognizing a pattern you have already met.
KeyTalkingPoints: The technical estate here is operated by partners and customers rather than by us, and there are far more customers per engineer than in Enterprise, so risk is found by pattern rather than by inspection. The problems worth tracking are the ones you have already diagnosed once: a configuration that fails under load, a version combination that breaks on upgrade, an integration that degrades quietly. Consumption movement belongs to the D-CSA and is not the engineer's signal. The intervention normally runs through whoever operates the solution. Facilitator note: the judgment here is about noticing and routing rather than fixing.
DiscussionQuestions:
How would you currently find out a customer's solution was in trouble?
Which technical problem have you now seen at more than one customer?
Who actually fixes it when you find one?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical problem you have seen at more than one customer.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which of your customers are running the configuration you already know is fragile?
Which of them has a partner who probably knows already?
What can you actually do about it from where you sit?
ListenFor: Listen for problems treated as one-offs when they have already recurred, for partner-operated estates assumed to be unmonitored, for engineers taking on a fix that belongs to whoever operates it, and for warnings sent without a route to action.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the exposed list to the one fix each person routes.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a recurring problem, use the last customer escalation and ask whether anything about it was predictable.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the customer each person is warning and who is actually going to fix it.
ReflectPrompt: Which problem had you already seen twice without treating it as a pattern?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, identify which of your customers are exposed to a technical problem you have already met elsewhere, and route one fix to whoever operates the solution.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the pattern, who was exposed, and where you routed it.

SessionIntroduction: This is the first of eight huddles, and the one with no AI activity in it. Today is about what the motion is and what it asks of you. Frontier Accelerator exists because we are asking customers to reshape how they work around AI, and that argument is stronger when we have done it ourselves first. That is what Customer Zero means here: we apply these tools to our own real work, and we are straight about where they help and where they do not.
KeyTalkingPoints:
Weekly and short, led by the manager with a facilitator. The cadence carries the motion, so if the slot has to move, move it rather than drop it.
Four principles hold every week: keep the weekly rhythm, learn from what colleagues have actually tried, ground every session in real work rather than hypothetical scenarios, and try something between huddles so there is an experience to bring back.
Every huddle from next week runs to the same shape, and the agenda and timings are set out on the huddle page: a short framing of why the topic matters, then sharing what you tried since last time, then hands-on work on a real scenario, then a close where you pick the one thing you will carry into the week.
Five roles make the motion work. The Leader connects it to strategy and clears barriers. The Manager owns the huddle and opens with the why. The Facilitator runs it and draws every voice in. The Team Member experiments in their own workflow and brings back wins and friction. The Coach reviews patterns across huddles and feeds insight back.
The journey ahead: this week you get grounded, weeks two to eight you build the habit on real work, week nine the team decides which habits stick and what comes next, and from week ten you choose your own topics.
You are here as a peer, not an expert. You do not need prior AI experience, and “I do not know” is a good answer.
Two things on feedback. The facilitator posts one question in the chat each week, asking how useful the huddle was on a scale of one to ten. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes to improve the sessions, so keep confidential detail out of the room, whether that is customer, partner, enrollment or commercial, and put product problems into the tool's own feedback control rather than here.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you deliberately avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted output in front of a customer?
What would make thirty minutes a week worth protecting for this?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: complete the baseline survey if it has been sent to you, confirm the huddle series is on your calendar, confirm you can open at least one of the tools named for your path, since the commitment at the end of this session runs in one of them, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. If your access is blocked, come anyway and say so, because that is a different problem from not being interested. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which work do you repeat every week without ever thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where does your judgment have to stay human no matter how good the output gets?
What would have to happen in these thirty minutes for you to want the next one?
ListenFor: Listen for unvoiced skepticism, for access blockers stated as disinterest, and for the assumption that this is a tool rollout. Listen for people describing only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat, because the recurring and unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping. Listen for anyone who thinks they need to be an AI expert to take part, and correct that in the room.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
FallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the conversation and record access blockers separately from interest, since they need different fixes. The discovery prompt runs in whichever tool the person already has. If the room stays quiet, start with your own example of work you repeat every week.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the discovery prompt below. Week one is for finding the recurring work worth handing to AI. Post the usefulness question in the chat before people leave.
ReflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
CommitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

“I am a [your role] at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with.”
BringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

SessionIntroduction: On these accounts the technical work is done by a partner you have no authority over, with no support agreement behind you. This session is about making a handover that actually gets acted on.
KeyTalkingPoints: Consumption execution in this segment runs through the D-CSA and partner delivery, particularly on non-Unified Azure. Unlike a Unified engagement there is no funded delivery vehicle and no contractual escalation route, so the handover has to stand on its own. Partner Center sits outside what our agents can reach, so partner-side progress returns through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center directly. CELA rules govern the exchange: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: the useful frame is that you are writing for a competent engineer who was not in any of your conversations.
DiscussionQuestions:
When you hand technical work to a partner, how do you find out whether it happened?
What do you end up doing yourself because handing it over felt slower?
What does a partner need from you that you usually leave out?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account where a partner is doing or should be doing the technical work.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What would this partner need to act on this without calling you?
How would you know in a month whether anything happened?
What are you holding onto that you should have handed over?
ListenFor: Listen for handovers that assume context the partner does not have, for work retained because delegating felt slower, for progress assumed from silence, and for detail being prepared that CELA rules exclude.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the handover to the signal each person will use to check it landed.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live handover, use the last one that stalled and work out what was missing from it.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is handing over and the signal they will check.
ReflectPrompt: What did you keep because explaining it felt like more work than doing it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, hand one piece of technical work to a partner in a form they can act on unaided, and write down the specific signal you will check to know whether it worked.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you handed over and what the signal showed.

SessionIntroduction: You are probably not coming back to this account. This session is about preparing for a conversation on that assumption.
KeyTalkingPoints: A Unified engagement supports an ongoing advisory relationship with recurring contact. At this coverage ratio and without that agreement, most customers get a single technical conversation and then nothing until something breaks. That changes the objective from building understanding over time to making one intervention that survives your absence. Facilitator note: the temptation is to cover everything because you may not be back, and that reliably produces a conversation the customer remembers nothing from.
DiscussionQuestions:
How many of your accounts have you spoken to more than once?
What happens at an account after you leave it?
When did you last try to cover everything in one meeting?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer you have a technical conversation coming up with.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the single thing this customer most needs to get right?
Who will be here after you are not?
What would still be true in six months if you did nothing else?
ListenFor: Listen for agendas that try to cover everything, for advice that depends on the architect returning, for no named owner on the customer or partner side, and for durable guidance never written down.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the single priority to what each person will leave behind.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has an upcoming conversation, use an account they have not revisited and ask what is still standing from the last one.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one thing each person is leaving behind and who is picking it up.
ReflectPrompt: Which of your advice quietly assumed you would be coming back?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, prepare one customer conversation around a single priority, and leave something written that a customer or partner could act on without you.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you left behind and who owns it now.

SessionIntroduction: Somebody else delivered most of what worked at your accounts. This session is about what you can honestly say about it.
KeyTalkingPoints: A Unified engagement leaves a delivery record - milestones, hours, an engagement manager - that can be pointed at. On non-Unified accounts none of that exists, so the evidence is telemetry plus whatever the partner is willing to share. Separate what was deployed from what is being used and from what the customer got value from; those are three different claims and only the first is reliably in the record. The renewal conversation belongs to the DAE and the CE, so evidence that stays with you does not reach it. Facilitator note: partner-delivered outcomes are the partner's to describe, and claiming them damages the relationship that is doing the work.
DiscussionQuestions:
When an account goes well, where is the proof?
How much of what worked was delivered by a partner?
Who asks you for value evidence, and when?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring two or three accounts where you believe the technical outcome was good.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What can you evidence about that outcome as opposed to believe?
Whose outcome is it to describe?
Who needs this before the renewal, and have they got it?
ListenFor: Listen for deployment presented as value, for partner-delivered outcomes claimed as ours, for evidence that exists only in the architect's head, and for renewals approaching with nobody having asked.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the evidence review to what each person passes on and to whom.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a clear success, use an account that renewed quietly and ask what evidence would have been available if anyone had wanted it.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is passing on and who is receiving it.
ReflectPrompt: Which good outcome would have gone unrecorded if nobody asked?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish what one account's technical outcome can actually be evidenced with, separate what the partner delivered, and send it to whoever owns the renewal.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you could evidence, what you could not, and who you sent it to.
