SessionIntroduction: Most roles here decide what to send out to a partner. You also have to decide what to do with what comes back the other way.
KeyTalkingPoints: Partner-originated demand arrives qualified to the partner's standard rather than ours, and the windows are already running: a partner has fourteen days to accept a referral before it expires, and sixty days to convert it before the system marks it lost. IP co-sell registration has its own conditions - the deal must be won on a Microsoft-managed account, be Azure IP co-sell eligible, be at least twenty-five thousand US dollars, and have a seventy-two hour gap between creation and being marked won. CELA rules limit what can be exchanged in either direction. Facilitator note: the honest difficulty here is that you often cannot verify what the partner is telling you, and deciding how much to invest on their word is the actual skill.
DiscussionQuestions:
How much of your pipeline originates with a partner rather than with us?
How do you decide whether to believe a partner's qualification?
When did a partner-sourced deal turn out not to be real?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity that came to you from a partner.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What do you actually know about this opportunity as opposed to what you were told?
What would you need to see to invest Microsoft resource behind it?
Which of your open partner-sourced items are closest to a window closing?
ListenFor: Listen for partner qualification accepted at face value, for registration conditions assumed rather than checked, for windows running unnoticed, and for reluctance to push back on a partner in case it damages the relationship.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the verification read to the one opportunity each person progresses or declines.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live partner-sourced opportunity, use the last one that went nowhere and work out what would have revealed it earlier.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the opportunity each person is progressing and the one they are declining.
ReflectPrompt: Which partner-sourced opportunity have you been carrying on trust?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish what can actually be verified about one partner-originated opportunity, check its registration conditions, and either progress it or tell the partner why you are not.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you could verify, what you could not, and what you decided.

SessionIntroduction: A cadence commitment across a portfolio of partners becomes a diary full of status calls unless somebody decides what each one is for. This session is about that decision.
KeyTalkingPoints: The partner rhythm in this segment includes a weekly partner meeting with the account roles and a minimum of monthly contact per partner seller, alongside deal clinics and the bi-weekly territory health review. Meeting a minimum is not the same as running a portfolio, and the partners who most need attention are rarely the ones who ask for it. Facilitator note: the useful distinction is between a meeting that needs an agenda because something has to be decided, and one that needs only a check-in because nothing has changed - treating them the same is what fills the week.
DiscussionQuestions:
How many partner meetings do you hold in a month, and how many changed anything?
Which partner have you not spoken to in longer than you should admit?
What makes a partner meeting worth having?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your partner list and roughly when you last spoke to each.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which of your partners has something that actually needs deciding this month?
Which are you meeting out of obligation?
Who is quietly getting no attention at all?
ListenFor: Listen for cadence treated as the objective rather than the floor, for the loudest partners absorbing the time, for meetings with no decision attached, and for the quiet partners going unmentioned.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the triage to the agenda each person will set for their one substantive meeting.
FallbackGuidance: If someone has few partners, work the last month of meetings and ask which produced a decision.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the partner each person is giving real time to and the ones they are handling lightly.
ReflectPrompt: Which partner has been getting your time because they ask for it rather than because they need it?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, triage three to five of your partners for the month, set a real agenda for the one meeting that needs a decision, and make sure your monthly contact commitment is met across the partner sellers you carry.
BringBackEvidence: Bring your triage and what the substantive meeting decided.

SessionIntroduction: When a partner closes and delivers, Microsoft largely stops seeing the customer. You are the only route back.
KeyTalkingPoints: In CSP the partner frequently leads the later stages and often closes, which means our record ends roughly where the customer's experience begins. The PSS has visibility into the partner relationship without owning execution, so the realistic goal is closing an information gap rather than driving an outcome. What the partner will tell you is governed by the CELA rules in both directions, and a partner is under no obligation to report customer outcomes to us at all. Facilitator note: the value of asking is as much about the partner relationship as about the answer - a partner who is asked how the customer is doing behaves differently from one who is only asked about pipeline.
DiscussionQuestions:
What do you know about customers your partners closed last quarter?
Who would tell you if one of them was unhappy?
When did you last ask a partner about a customer rather than about a deal?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring two or three deals a partner closed in the last few quarters.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What does our record actually show about these customers since the close?
What would you want to know that only the partner can tell you?
What is in it for the partner to tell you?
ListenFor: Listen for usage data mistaken for customer satisfaction, for the assumption that silence means success, for questions framed as inspection rather than as interest, and for renewal dates approaching with nobody having asked anything.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the visibility gap to the one question each person will put to a partner.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has recent closed deals, use a renewal that was lost and ask when the first sign was available.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the partner each person is asking and the question they are asking.
ReflectPrompt: Which customer do you know nothing about since the day it closed?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, map what our record can and cannot tell you about customers a partner closed, and ask one partner directly how a specific customer is getting on.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you could not see, what the partner told you, and whether it surprised you.

SessionIntroduction: Every deal meets the policy questions eventually. This session is about meeting them while the structure is still a question rather than a commitment.
KeyTalkingPoints: Policy, licensing and eligibility interpretation always routes to the authoritative owner rather than to an agent or to your own reading. In this segment a substantial share transacts through CSP, which carries its own eligibility conditions - Modern Commerce and an accepted agreement with a pre-existing partner billing relationship, with legacy arrangements excluded - so the route matters as much as the structure. Facilitator note: the failure mode is not getting a policy answer wrong, it is answering at all when the question belonged to somebody else, because an answer from the commercial person is treated as authoritative.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did a policy question last surface too late to change anything?
Which questions do you find yourself answering that you should be routing?
How long does an authoritative answer actually take to get?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live deal where the commercial structure is not yet fixed.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What in this deal has an eligibility or licensing condition attached to it?
Which of those can you answer from approved guidance, and which need the owner?
What would it cost to find out at approval instead of now?
ListenFor: Listen for policy answered from memory or from a previous deal, for eligibility assumed because a similar customer qualified, for CSP conditions treated as the same as direct, and for questions deferred because getting an answer feels slow.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the question list to the one each person will route today.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live deal, use the last one where a policy issue surfaced late and work out when it first became answerable.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the question each person is routing and who they are routing it to.
ReflectPrompt: Which policy question have you been answering yourself?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, run one live deal against the policy and eligibility questions it will face, and route every unresolved one to its authoritative owner rather than carrying it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the question you routed and what the answer changed.

SessionIntroduction: In this segment the negotiation is frequently conducted by a partner. Your concession logic has to work when applied by somebody who does not report to you.
KeyTalkingPoints: The Commercial Executive owns concession authority and the commercial boundary, but in a partner-transacted deal the conversation with the customer is often the partner's. That changes the artifact from a negotiation plan you will execute into a boundary somebody else has to hold. CELA rules govern what can be shared with the partner: personal data, screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: the useful question in the room is what happens to your boundary when you are not there to defend it.
DiscussionQuestions:
On your last partner-transacted deal, who actually did the negotiating?
What did you concede that you had not planned to?
How do you tell a partner what they cannot offer without telling them your floor?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live deal heading toward a negotiation.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What can be conceded on this deal without approval, and what cannot?
How does the partner know where that line is?
What would trigger you to escalate rather than concede?
ListenFor: Listen for concession authority assumed rather than confirmed, for boundaries that exist only in the CE's head, for partner briefings that reveal the floor, and for escalation triggers defined after the pressure has started.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the boundary to how each person will communicate it to the partner.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live negotiation, use one that conceded more than intended and work out where the boundary failed.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the boundary each person is setting and how the partner will learn it.
ReflectPrompt: Where has a concession been made in your name that you would not have made?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, write down the concession logic and authority limits for one live deal, name the escalation trigger, and brief the partner on what cannot be conceded without revealing your floor.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you told the partner and whether the boundary held.

SessionIntroduction: Approvals discovered one at a time cost a week each. This session is about finding them all at once, including the ones that are not yours to obtain.
KeyTalkingPoints: On a partner-transacted deal the approval path runs across two organizations, and the steps on the partner side are visible only through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center rather than through our own systems. Approval lead times drift with quarter load, so a plan built on last quarter's turnaround will miss. Facilitator note: the distinction worth drawing is between an approval you can obtain, one you can only request, and one the partner has to obtain from their own side - all three look the same on a plan and behave completely differently.
DiscussionQuestions:
How do you currently find out what approvals a structure will need?
Which approvals on your last deal were discovered late?
What happens when the partner needs an approval from their own organization?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one deal with a commercial structure that needs approving.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which approvals does this structure trigger, and who owns each?
Which are genuinely sequential and which have you been treating as sequential out of habit?
What does the partner have to obtain that you cannot?
ListenFor: Listen for approval owners named by role rather than by person, for parallel approvals treated as a chain, for partner-side steps assumed to be quick, and for evidence requirements discovered at submission.
SuggestedTransitions:
Move from the mapped path to the one approval each person will start today.
Customer Zero cue - use only if it happens: when someone reverts, rejects or overrides what the agent produced, stop and name it. Ask what the agent could not see. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes, so what is said here does reach us - keep customer-confidential detail out of it.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live deal, reconstruct the approval path of the last one that slipped and identify where the time went.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the approval each person is starting and what evidence it needs.
ReflectPrompt: Which approval did you assume somebody else was handling?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, map the approval path for one deal with a named owner and the required evidence for each step, mark which belong to the partner, and start the one on the critical path.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the map and what you found was missing from it.

SessionIntroduction: A commercial structure that cannot be explained without you in the room will not get approved when you are not. This session is about making one reviewable.
KeyTalkingPoints: In this segment the CE is frequently absent from the conversation where the structure is actually decided - the partner is in the room and the approver reads a document. That makes the written case the product, not a summary of it. Separate the three things an approver needs: what decision they are being asked to make, whether the numbers can be checked, and what is being asserted without support. Facilitator note: the instinct is to make the case persuasive. Push the group towards making it inspectable instead, because an approver who cannot verify a figure will not approve around it.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did an approval last stall on something other than the merits?
What in your last commercial case could the approver not have checked?
Who has to be able to read this when you are not there?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one commercial structure you have agreed and still need to take to approval.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What exactly is the approver being asked to decide?
Which figure in this could someone else not verify?
What have you asserted that you have not shown?
ListenFor: Listen for cases that argue rather than evidence, for figures whose source nobody can name, for judgments stated as facts, and for people describing what they would say in the room when they will not be in the room.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the narrative to the one gap each person will close before sending it.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live structure awaiting approval, use the last one that was approved and ask what the approver had to take on trust.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the single unevidenced claim each person is going to close before their case goes out.
ReflectPrompt: What in your last approval request did the approver have to take on trust?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, write the decision narrative for one commercial structure, have it read back for unsupported claims, and close the gap on the central one.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the ask as you stated it, the gap that came back, and what you changed.

SessionIntroduction: Architecture in this segment is judged by whether it still works six months after you have moved on. This session is about designing for that.
KeyTalkingPoints: A DCSA carries a portfolio of non-unified customers - no dedicated support relationship, often no in-house platform team, and frequently a partner doing the implementation. That changes what a good design is. The elegant option that assumes someone will tune it is worse than the plain option that runs untouched. Separate the design decisions that need your expertise from the ones the customer or partner will end up making anyway, and make the second group hard to get wrong. Facilitator note: the instinct is to compare architectures on capability. Push the group to compare them on what happens when nobody is watching.
DiscussionQuestions:
Who is actually going to build this?
What does this design assume somebody will maintain?
What breaks first if nobody touches it for six months?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one architecture you are designing or reviewing now, and know who will implement it.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What does this design assume about the people running it?
Which decision here did you make because it was right, and which because it was familiar?
What would you simplify if you knew nobody would ever tune it?
ListenFor: Listen for designs justified by capability rather than by operability, for assumptions about customer skill that nobody has tested, for a partner implementer who has not been consulted, and for support models being assumed rather than confirmed.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the design to the single assumption each person will go and verify.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live design, take an architecture already deployed on one of their accounts and ask what it assumed that turned out not to be true.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one operability assumption each person will confirm with the implementer this week.
ReflectPrompt: Which of your designs needed you more than it should have?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one design to the person who will build it and confirm they can operate it without you.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the assumption you tested and what the implementer said.

SessionIntroduction: Every consumption problem has a technical cause that appeared first. This session is about catching it at that point rather than at the review.
KeyTalkingPoints: Across a portfolio of this size nobody can inspect accounts individually, so technical risk is found either by a signal or by a complaint. The gap between those two is where the DCSA earns their place. Distinguish three things that look identical from outside: a workload that was never fully deployed, one that was deployed and abandoned, and one that is working but small. Only the first two are yours. Facilitator note: this session pairs with a standing check - the point is not the one-off scan but the rhythm that replaces it.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did you last find a technical problem before the customer did?
What told you about your last consumption drop, and how late was it?
Which of your accounts could be in trouble without you knowing?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: know which consumption or usage view you can actually reach for your portfolio.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the earliest signal you could realistically have seen?
Which risks here would the customer dispute?
What would you want to be told automatically every week?
ListenFor: Listen for risk lists with no owner, for signals being read as problems without a technical hypothesis, for people describing manual checks they know they will not sustain, and for accounts nobody has looked at in months being called healthy.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the scan to the standing check that means they do not have to remember to run it.
FallbackGuidance: If consumption data is not reachable, use support and service records instead and ask what those alone can and cannot tell you.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the risk they are acting on and confirm their standing check is running.
ReflectPrompt: What did you find late that you could have found early?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, start one technical intervention and leave a standing check running on your portfolio.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the risk you acted on, what the check has surfaced since, and whether any of it was new.

SessionIntroduction: Expansion in this segment is found in the telemetry of what is already working, not built in a deck. This session is about reading that evidence.
KeyTalkingPoints: A DCSA is accountable for uncovering the next logical workload, but not for selling it - that boundary matters and gets blurred under pressure. Readiness has three parts and all three have to hold: the customer is succeeding with something adjacent, they have the technical capacity to take on more, and somebody on their side wants it. Two out of three produces a stalled deployment that damages the account you were trying to grow. Facilitator note: watch for expansion proposed from what Microsoft wants to sell rather than from what the customer has proven they can run.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your accounts is genuinely succeeding with something right now?
What did your last expansion attempt assume that was not true?
Who on the customer side would actually want the next workload?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account where a workload is deployed and working.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the evidence this customer is ready rather than just suitable?
Who asked for this, or did we?
What would have to be true technically before this could start?
ListenFor: Listen for expansion built on product fit rather than customer readiness, for deployed being read as adopted, for no named customer sponsor, and for DCSAs carrying the commercial conversation themselves rather than handing it over.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the hypothesis to who owns the conversation and what they need from it.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a succeeding workload, work the opposite way: take a stalled deployment and ask what would have had to be true for it to have worked.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the owner of each expansion conversation and what evidence goes with it.
ReflectPrompt: Which expansion did you propose that the customer was not ready for?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, evidence one expansion hypothesis and hand it to whoever owns the commercial conversation.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the readiness evidence, who you handed it to, and what they did with it.

SessionIntroduction: The same technical problem arrives at this team repeatedly wearing different customer names. This session is about answering it once.
KeyTalkingPoints: Reuse fails for a predictable reason: the asset gets saved and the context does not. Another engineer finds a script or a design and cannot tell what it assumed, so they rebuild it, and now there are two. The reusable unit is the artifact plus its constraints - what it was built for, what it depends on, and where it does not apply. Sanitization matters more here than in Enterprise because at this volume an asset gets reused many times before anyone reviews it. Facilitator note: the community hubs already hold field-contributed assets; check before building.
DiscussionQuestions:
What have you built more than once?
What have you looked for and failed to find?
What would somebody need to know before reusing your last piece of work?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one artifact you built recently that you think somebody else could use.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Could somebody use this without talking to you?
What does it assume that is not written down?
Where would this be wrong to apply?
ListenFor: Listen for assets shared without their constraints, for customer-identifying detail left in, for reuse being treated as filing rather than as writing, and for people describing things they rebuilt that already existed somewhere.
SuggestedTransitions:
Move from the artifact to where it will live and who will find it.
Customer Zero cue - use only if it happens: when someone reverts, rejects or overrides what the agent produced, stop and name it. Ask what the agent could not see. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes, so what is said here does reach us - keep customer-confidential detail out of it.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has an artifact, use the last question they answered twice and capture the answer instead.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming where each asset is going and who else has been told it exists.
ReflectPrompt: What did you rebuild this quarter that already existed?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, publish one asset with its limitations stated, and tell the team where it is.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the asset, where it now lives, and whether anyone has used it.

SessionIntroduction: When a partner-led deal stops moving, the cause is usually that somebody on the partner side is not confident enough to take the next technical step. This session is about finding that and fixing it properly.
KeyTalkingPoints: This is the one part of the DSE path with no Enterprise equivalent, and it carries a genuine tension: the fastest way to unblock a partner-led deal is to do the technical work yourself, and that is exactly what prevents the partner ever becoming self-sufficient. The distinction to hold is between a gap in knowledge, which enablement fixes, and a gap in capacity, which it does not. Facilitator note: partner-side detail is limited in our systems, so most of the evidence here comes from what the partner tells you and how their deals actually behave.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your partner-led deals keep needing you?
What do you end up explaining more than once?
Is the partner missing knowledge, or missing people?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner-led opportunity that has stalled or that keeps returning to you.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What exactly can the partner not do yet?
Is that knowledge, capacity, or willingness?
What would let them do this without you next time?
ListenFor: Listen for DSEs absorbing partner work and calling it enablement, for capability gaps described as attitude problems, for enablement with no owner or date, and for the same partner appearing behind several stalled deals.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the gap to the specific enablement action and who owns it on the partner side.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a stalled partner deal, use the last one they unblocked and ask what would have happened if they had been unavailable.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the enablement action, its owner on the partner side, and the date.
ReflectPrompt: What are you doing for a partner that they should be able to do themselves?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, name one partner technical gap and agree an enablement action with a named owner and a date.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the gap, the action agreed, and whether the partner did it.

SessionIntroduction: Competitive positions usually fail because they answer a comparison the customer was not making. This session is about finding the real one.
KeyTalkingPoints: A DSS carries a solution area across many accounts, so the same competitive conversation recurs with small variations - which makes it worth getting right once. Three things get confused: what we do better, what the customer values, and what they are actually comparing us to. Only the overlap of all three is a differentiator. Being honest about where a competitor is stronger is what makes the rest of the position credible, and sellers consistently underrate how obvious the omission is to a customer who has already seen the other vendor. Facilitator note: push for the specific competitor and the specific criteria, not a general positioning discussion.
DiscussionQuestions:
What is this customer actually comparing us to?
Which of our advantages have they told you they care about?
Where is the competitor genuinely better?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity where a competitor is involved and you know who it is.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What are the customer's own decision criteria, in their words?
Which differentiator survives contact with those criteria?
What will you concede, and when?
ListenFor: Listen for feature comparisons standing in for customer criteria, for competitor weaknesses asserted without a source, for positions that concede nothing, and for the same objection appearing across several accounts without anyone having prepared for it.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the position to the one objection each person will prepare properly.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live competitive deal, take the objection they hear most often across the solution area and build the position around that instead.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the objection each person will prepare and the evidence they will bring to it.
ReflectPrompt: Which competitive claim have you made that you could not evidence?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one competitive position with a customer and record which part of it actually landed.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the position, what the customer responded to, and what you dropped.

SessionIntroduction: In this segment nobody is assigned to your opportunity. Everything you need comes from someone who is also doing their own job. This session is about asking well.
KeyTalkingPoints: An ask that describes a situation gets sympathy; an ask that describes a specific task with a date gets done. The three things that make an ask answerable are what exactly is needed, by when, and what happens if it does not arrive - the last one is almost always omitted and is what moves an ask up someone's list. Separate asks that need a person from asks that need a decision, because they go to different places and have different lead times. Facilitator note: watch for people who have absorbed a task themselves rather than asking, and ask what that cost them.
DiscussionQuestions:
What are you doing yourself that you should have asked for?
What did you last ask for that never arrived?
Would the person receiving your ask know exactly what to do?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity where you need support you have not yet asked for.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What exactly do you need, and by when?
Who specifically, not which team?
What happens to the deal if it does not come?
ListenFor: Listen for asks addressed to a team rather than a person, for needs described as context rather than as tasks, for no date, and for people who have stopped asking because previous asks went unanswered.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the ask to the standing check that tells them when it has gone quiet.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live need, use the last support ask that went unanswered and rewrite it as it should have been sent.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each ask has a person, a task and a date, and that a check is running.
ReflectPrompt: What did you stop asking for because it never came?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, send one specific support ask and set a check that tells you if it goes unanswered.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the ask, whether it was answered, and how long it took.

SessionIntroduction: Partner capability and partner capacity look identical from the outside and fail in completely different ways. This session is about telling them apart before you route work.
KeyTalkingPoints: Capability is whether they know how; capacity is whether they have anyone free. Enablement fixes the first and does nothing for the second, which is why so much partner enablement is politely attended and never applied. The evidence available to us is partial - program participation and past delivery tell you about capability, and almost nothing tells you about capacity, which usually has to be asked. Facilitator note: a partner rarely says no to work, so absence of refusal is not evidence of readiness.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which of your partners have you routed work to without checking?
When a partner-led engagement last went wrong, was it skill or bandwidth?
How would you know a partner was overcommitted?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner you are currently routing work to or considering.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Is this a knowledge gap or a people gap?
What evidence do you have, and what are you assuming?
What would you have to see to route confidently?
ListenFor: Listen for capability judged from the partner's own claims, for capacity never being asked about, for program certifications treated as delivery evidence, and for partners being chosen by relationship rather than by readiness.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the assessment to the specific action and who on the partner side owns it.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live routing decision, use a partner engagement that went badly and work out which of the two gaps it actually was.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the gap, the closing action, its partner-side owner and the date.
ReflectPrompt: Which partner have you kept using out of habit rather than evidence?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, assess one partner's readiness properly and agree one closing action with them.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the gap you found, what you agreed, and whether the partner acted.

SessionIntroduction: Partners agree to a great deal in meetings and act on very little of it. The difference is almost always whether the ask made sense in their economics.
KeyTalkingPoints: You influence without authority across more partners than you can meet, so each conversation has to carry weight. A partner's economics are not a mystery - margin, utilization of their consultants, recurring revenue and how quickly they get paid - and framing an ask against any of those changes the response. The most common failure is a conversation that reports Microsoft's view of the partnership back to a partner who experiences it completely differently. Facilitator note: Know Your Partner is purpose-built for assembling this briefing; confirm access before relying on it.
DiscussionQuestions:
What does this partner actually make money on?
What did you last ask a partner to do, and did they?
What would they say the partnership is currently worth to them?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner you have a conversation coming up with.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is in this for their business specifically?
What is your one ask?
What will they raise that you have not prepared for?
ListenFor: Listen for asks framed in Microsoft targets, for partner economics being assumed rather than known, for several asks where there should be one, and for briefings that report performance without proposing anything.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the briefing to rehearsing the one ask and the objection they expect.
FallbackGuidance: If Know Your Partner is not available to you, assemble the same evidence from partner performance reporting and use the rest of the workflow unchanged.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each person has one ask, framed in partner economics, and has rehearsed the objection.
ReflectPrompt: When did a partner agree with you and then not act?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, have one partner conversation with a single ask framed in their economics, and record what they committed to.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the ask, what they committed to, and whether it happened.

SessionIntroduction: Investment in SME&C is not one thing. This session is about picking the right route before you build anything.
KeyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. For a DSS the relevant question is usually whether the solution-area opportunity is large enough to carry direct investment or whether it belongs in a partner-led or voucher motion. Facilitator note: resist letting this become an ECIF mechanics session - the mechanics only matter once the route is right.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which investment route do you reach for by default?
When did an investment request last fail, and at what stage?
Who tells you whether something is eligible?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one solution-area opportunity where customer investment might help.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the barrier the investment would actually remove?
Which route fits the size and shape of this deal?
What do you not know about eligibility?
ListenFor: Listen for one route being used for everything, for eligibility being assumed from a previous deal, for investment proposed before the barrier is clear, and for people who have stopped requesting because a past request failed late.
SuggestedTransitions:
Move from the route to the eligibility question each person will route to an owner.
Customer Zero cue - use only if it happens: when someone reverts, rejects or overrides what the agent produced, stop and name it. Ask what the agent could not see. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes, so what is said here does reach us - keep customer-confidential detail out of it.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live candidate, take the last investment request that failed and work out which route it should have taken.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each person has a route and one eligibility question sent to a named owner.
ReflectPrompt: What did you last build that turned out to be the wrong vehicle?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, match one opportunity to an investment route and get one eligibility question answered authoritatively.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the route you chose, the question you asked and the answer you got.

SessionIntroduction: The investment routes that matter most in this segment run through partners. This session is about using them deliberately.
KeyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. For a PSS the additional dimension is that partner-led routes place obligations on the PARTNER - nomination, activity completion, evidence - and a partner who does not know what they have signed up to is the most common reason a partner-led investment produces nothing. Facilitator note: the partner's incentive under each route is worth naming explicitly; it is rarely the same as ours.
DiscussionQuestions:
Which partner-led routes do you actually use?
When did a partner-led program last produce nothing, and why?
Does the partner know what the program requires of them?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner and one opportunity where investment could help.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What does this route require the partner to do?
What does the partner get out of it?
Who is tracking whether they do it?
ListenFor: Listen for partner obligations being assumed rather than agreed, for programs nominated and never started, for the partner's incentive being taken for granted, and for PSS carrying activity that the program expects the partner to carry.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the route to the specific obligation the partner has agreed to and the date.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live candidate, use a partner program that was nominated and never completed and work out where it stalled.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each person has a route and a partner-side obligation agreed with a name and a date.
ReflectPrompt: Which partner program did you nominate and never follow up?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, match one partner opportunity to a route and confirm with the partner what it requires of them.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the route, what the partner agreed to, and whether they started.

SessionIntroduction: Customer investment reaches your role even though you do not own the request. This session is about the part that is yours.
KeyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. A DAE does not own investment requests but meets the barriers that investment removes, across more accounts than anyone else. The value is in recognition and routing rather than in submission. Facilitator note: keep this session on the role's own contribution rather than letting it drift into submission mechanics owned elsewhere.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where have you seen investment help, and where have you seen it wasted?
What does your role actually contribute to an investment decision?
Who owns the request once you have raised it?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one situation where customer investment is or was in play.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the barrier, precisely?
What is yours to decide here and what is not?
What would you need to see to be confident?
ListenFor: Listen for investment proposed as a discount by another name, for barriers that are really timing, and for DAEs building requests themselves rather than routing them.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the assessment to the one thing each person routes or confirms this week.
FallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live case, use the last investment situation they encountered and work through what their role should have contributed.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person will route or confirm, and to whom.
ReflectPrompt: When did you last see investment used for something it could not fix?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one investment situation and contribute the part your role owns.
BringBackEvidence: Bring what you found, who you took it to, and what happened.

SessionIntroduction: A closed-won record carries your number whether or not you were the one who set it. Closes arrive through your own work, through automation, and through other people acting on the account. This session is about reading your own recent closes and deciding which ones you can stand behind.
KeyTalkingPoints:
A wrong close raises no error and blocks nothing. It stays in the book until somebody has to explain it, and by then the context has gone.
The test is not whether the record is well-formed. It is whether the value, the products and the date describe what was actually sold.
Your account knowledge is the input here, not the verdict. A correction made without the contract in front of you replaces one wrong record with another.
Finding nothing is a real result. Say so in the room rather than treating the exercise as having failed.
DiscussionQuestions:
When did you last read your own closed-won list rather than your open pipeline?
If a close in your book were wrong, how would you find out?
Which part of a closed record would you struggle to explain in a review?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm you can open Sales Agent, and choose a recent period short enough to read in one sitting. Bring what you remember about the accounts in it, because that memory is the instrument this exercise runs on.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which close in your list did you not recognize straight away?
What in that record does not match what you remember selling?
Is this one yours to correct, or does it need somebody else?
ListenFor: Listen for sellers scrolling past records they do not recognize because the totals look right. Listen for “that must have been the partner” or “that came from the team” offered as an explanation rather than as something to check. Listen for reluctance to raise a close that flatters the number, and for the assumption that a well-formed record is a correct one.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the list of closes nobody could account for to the single record each person will resolve, and how they will resolve it.
FallbackGuidance: If Sales Agent access is not available, run it from a report export or the opportunity list, since the exercise is reading your own closes rather than the tool that surfaces them. If nobody finds an unexplained close, use the time to ask how they would notice one.
WrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the one record they will resolve, and which of the four it is: accepted, corrected by them, routed to somebody who can act on it, or held pending a specific check.
ReflectPrompt: What did you find in your own closed book that you had not looked at before? What would have to be true for you to notice it sooner next time?
CommitPrompt: Before the next huddle, resolve one closed-won record you could not account for: accept it, correct it, route it to whoever can act on it, or write down the specific thing you need to check.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the record, what you could not account for, what you did about it, and whether it turned out to be yours to correct.

SessionIntroduction: Satisfaction is decided during the delivery, not at the survey. Today is about reading it early enough to act.
KeyTalkingPoints:
The customer already knows how they feel. The survey only tells us.
Responsiveness, clarity and expectation-setting move scores as much as technical outcomes do.
A satisfaction risk you cannot evidence is a feeling. Name what you saw.
DiscussionQuestions:
Where in a current delivery would the customer say we are harder to work with than we need to be?
Which satisfaction signal have you noticed and not acted on?
What would this customer say if they were asked today rather than at the end?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live delivery, any customer feedback or escalation on it, and the moment you would least like the customer to remember.
FacilitatorQuestions:
Which delivery are you least confident about, and what is the evidence rather than the feeling?
What would the customer say we did slowly or explained badly?
Which satisfaction risk is yours to fix and which belongs to another role?
ListenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: satisfaction inferred from the absence of complaints; technical success treated as the whole of the customer experience; risks named without a specific moment behind them; and anything the CSA plans to absorb that belongs to the CSAM or to delivery.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from the general idea of satisfaction to one live delivery and the specific moment that would show up in the score.
FallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized delivery. Do not speculate about individual customer contacts or attribute dissatisfaction to named people.
WrapUpGuidance: Name one satisfaction risk, the evidence behind it, and the action you will take before the delivery closes.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Take one live delivery, name the satisfaction risk you would least like to see in the survey, and act on it this week.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the risk you named and what changed after you acted.

SessionIntroduction: You get called in when you are the person who can answer the question. Today is about deciding which questions those will be.
KeyTalkingPoints:
Technical credibility is set by the customer's roadmap, not by our product releases.
The gap worth closing is the one the customer hits next, not the most interesting one.
Being able to say what you do not know is part of being trusted, not the opposite of it.
DiscussionQuestions:
What will this customer be building in six months that you could not advise on today?
Where have you been the bottleneck because the answer had to come from someone else?
Which technical topic do you avoid, and what does avoiding it cost?
PreparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer, what you know of their technical direction, and one question you were recently unable to answer.
FacilitatorQuestions:
What is the next technical decision this customer faces, and could you hold that conversation today?
Which gap is real and which is imagined?
What is the smallest step that would make you credible on it?
ListenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: gaps chosen by personal interest rather than by customer need; plans to learn everything rather than one thing; and cases where the honest answer is to bring in a specialist rather than close the gap personally.
SuggestedTransitions: Move from general capability to one customer, one upcoming technical decision, and one gap.
FallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized customer. Keep the focus on technical direction rather than commercial detail.
WrapUpGuidance: Name the technical gap you are closing, why this customer makes it urgent, and the first step.
ReflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
CommitPrompt: Name one technical topic your customer will need you on within the next two quarters, and take the first step toward being able to defend it.
BringBackEvidence: Bring the gap you named and what you did about it.
